Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: read only the last two sentences of paragraph A. What will the essay argue? Tick one.
happiness cannot be measured   well-being is more a way of living than a feeling   money brings happiness

Feeling Good or Living Well? Rethinking Happiness

An academic essay · Psychology and society · about 620 words · C1 · written for this book

AFew goals are as universal as happiness. Parents wish it for their children, advertisers promise it with every product, and governments increasingly claim to pursue it on behalf of their citizens. Yet the word itself is surprisingly slippery. In everyday speech, “happiness” may refer to a passing mood after good news, or to a deep sense that one’s life is going well. Researchers in psychology and economics therefore tend to prefer the broader term “well-being”, which covers both how people feel and how they function. This essay argues that well-being is better understood as a way of living than as a feeling, and that this distinction matters for individuals and policymakers alike. It first examines the two main traditions of thought, then considers how well-being can be measured, and finally asks what a society might learn from the difference.

BThe idea that happiness has two faces is far from new. One tradition, often called hedonic, sees a good life as one with as much pleasure and as little pain as possible. Another, which goes back to Aristotle’s notion of eudaimonia, holds that people flourish when they develop their abilities and live according to virtue. In the medieval Islamic world, the philosopher al-Farabi, who was born in Central Asia, wrote that true happiness is reached not alone but within a virtuous community. On this view, a pleasant afternoon is welcome, but it is not the whole story.

CModern research has, to a large extent, confirmed that both dimensions are real. Many studies suggest that people’s daily moods and their overall judgement of their lives do not always move together. A young doctor working long night shifts may feel exhausted for months, yet describe her life as deeply meaningful. Conversely, a person with a comfortable routine and few worries may report frequent pleasant feelings while sensing that something important is missing.

DMeasuring well-being is therefore more difficult than measuring income. Because both feelings and judgements are subjective, researchers usually rely on surveys that ask people to rate their life satisfaction, their emotions on a particular day, or their sense of purpose. Critics point out that answers can be affected by the weather, the order of the questions, or cultural habits of modesty. Nevertheless, when such surveys are designed carefully and repeated over time, they can serve as useful indicators alongside economic data. Several countries now publish official well-being statistics, and Bhutan has long promoted the idea of “Gross National Happiness” as an alternative to judging progress by economic growth alone.

Paragraph A is a door. Count the steps from wide to narrow.
Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 4 · Practical class 31
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

EThe distinction also has practical consequences. If happiness simply means feeling good, the quickest route to it might be entertainment, shopping or endless scrolling. If, however, well-being means living well, then relationships, health, meaningful work and a sense of belonging become central. This may help to explain why materialism is often associated with lower rather than higher life satisfaction: possessions can bring pleasure, but they rarely sustain fulfilment.

FUzbek culture offers a useful illustration. Traditions such as haşar, in which neighbours gather to help build a house or clean a street, rarely make anyone comfortable: the work is hard and dusty. Yet many participants remember such days with pride, because they combine effort, purpose and community. In the language of research, they add little to momentary pleasure but a great deal to resilience and belonging.

GIn conclusion, happiness is best seen not as a single feeling to be chased but as a pattern of living to be built. Individuals who understand this may choose differently between a new phone and an evening with friends; governments may look beyond income when they judge whether a country is truly progressing. Feeling good matters, but living well matters more.

Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on paragraph A (the door), Group B on B–D (ideas and measurement), Group C on E–G (consequences). Each group draws its part as one floor of a minaret on a card, then teaches it to a new mixed group in 60 seconds.

Language toolkit: from wide to narrow

10 MIN

A good introduction is a funnel: each sentence is narrower than the last.

Notice find it

Find these phrases in paragraph A and complete them.

1. Few goals are universal happiness.

2. the word itself is surprisingly slippery.

3. In everyday speech, “happiness” may a passing mood …

4. … the broader term “well-being”, covers both how people feel and how they function.

5. This essay that well-being is better understood as a way of living …

6. It examines …, considers …, and asks …

The funnel language rule
StepLanguageExample
GeneralFew … are as … as … · It is widely accepted that …Few goals are as old as this one.
NarrowYet / However, … · This is especially true of …This is especially true of students.
DefineX refers to … · In this essay, X is understood as …Here, well-being refers to …
ThesisThis essay argues that … · It will be argued that …It will be argued that …
RoadmapIt first …, then …, and finally … · It begins by + -ingIt begins by examining …

Three rules

  • A thesis is a claim, not a topic: This essay is about happiness. ✗ → This essay argues that happiness depends on relationships. ✓
  • Roadmap verbs are parallel: It first examines …, then considers …, and finally asks … ✓ · then considering ✗
  • Narrow step by step: each sentence is more specific than the last. Never begin with Since the dawn of time …
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence

2. In this essay I want to tell about happiness.
3. It first examines income, then considering health.
4. It will be argued that the friendship.
5. Since the beginning of humanity, people want joy.

Level up: the C1 thesis

CONTINUED

A B2 thesis takes a side. A C1 thesis takes a side and shows that the writer has seen the other one — with a precise key term and exactly the right strength.

ToolPhrasesExample
Concession in the door
admit, then claim		While …, this essay contends that … · Although …, it will be argued that …While income matters, this essay contends that relationships matter more.
Hedging
the right strength		largely · to a considerable extent · tends to · arguablyWell-being depends largely on the quality of our relationships.
Nominalisation
verb → noun		pursue → the pursuit of · measure → the measurement of · satisfy → satisfactionPeople pursue happiness. → The pursuit of happiness shapes many choices.
Precise definition
fix the key term		X is understood here as … · X is taken to mean … · X denotes …In this essay, well-being is taken to mean long-term life satisfaction.

The Blueprint: the foundation and the door

10 MIN

For the next fifteen stops you build one tall minaret of research, like the Kalon minaret in Bukhara. A minaret starts with a foundation and a door; an academic essay starts with an introduction. It takes your reader from common ground to your exact claim.

Wide at the bottom, narrow at the door: each sentence is more specific than the one before.

Part of the minaretPart of the introductionWhat goes insideWords
FoundationGeneral statementa calm claim that most readers accept≈ 20
Outer archBackgroundnarrow to your topic: why does it matter now, and here?≈ 30–40
Inner archFocus + key termthe problem or debate; what your key word means in this essay≈ 30
The doorThesisyour arguable claim, often with the main reasons≈ 30
Floor guideRoadmapthe order of the body paragraphs, in parallel verbs≈ 20

Rule of thumb: the introduction is about 10–15% of the whole essay.

Compare it think
Essay · Stop 7 (hovli)Opinion essay · Stop 8 (madrasa)Academic essay · Stop 31 (minaret)
Way inhook → background → thesishook → background → thesisgeneral → background → focus → thesis → roadmap
Voice“I” is fineIn my opinion, …impersonal: This essay argues …
Extras—two reasons in the thesisa defined key term + a roadmap

Walk through the door

CONTINUED
Task: “Money can buy happiness.” Discuss. Two students wrote an introduction. Read both. (Both versions were written for this book.)

Version 1 · a door without a foundation

(1) Since the dawn of time, people have wanted to be happy. (2) Money is very important in our modern life. (3) Some people say money can buy happiness, some people say it cannot. (4) In this essay I will talk about money and happiness and give my opinion.

Version 2 · the model annotated
Foundation
Few questions have occupied philosophers, economists and ordinary families as persistently as the link between money and happiness.
Outer arch
As living standards change, many young people can now afford comforts that their grandparents could only imagine, from smartphones to holidays abroad.
Inner arch
Yet it remains unclear whether these comforts make people more satisfied with their lives. In this essay, happiness refers not only to pleasant feelings but to overall life satisfaction.
The door
It will be argued that money contributes to happiness up to the point where basic needs and security are met, but that beyond this point relationships and a sense of purpose matter considerably more.
Floor guide
The essay first examines how income protects people from stress, then considers the limits of material comfort, and finally discusses what this means for young people choosing a career.

Announcement → Thesis

8 MIN

Weak introductions say what the essay is about. Strong ones say what it will argue. Turn each weak sentence into a thesis: a clear, arguable claim in calm academic language.

@essay_draft_1 · MondayIn this essay I will talk about happiness and social media.
→
This essay argues that heavy social media use can reduce young people’s well-being, although it also offers new ways to stay connected.
@happy_hamid · 5 minmoney = happiness. end of discussion 💸
→
@essay_draft_2 · TuesdayFamily is very important for the happiness of every person.
→
@tired_sevara · 1 hsome ppl say work makes u happy, some say no 🤷 who knows
→

Tool tips: This essay argues that … · It will be argued that … · While …, … · up to a point · more … than … · depends less on … than on …

Phrase bank use these
JobB2 · safeC1 · upgrade
Lay the foundationIt is widely accepted that …Few … are as … as … · … has long been seen as …
Raise the outer archIn recent years, … · Today, …This is especially true of … · As … changes, …
Fit the inner archIn this essay, X means …Yet it remains unclear whether … · X is taken to mean …
Open the doorThis essay argues that … · It will be argued that …While …, this essay contends that …
Hang the floor guideIt first …, then …, and finally …The essay begins by + -ing … and then turns to …

Common traps

✗ Nowadays, in our modern world, everybody wants happiness.
✓ Happiness is a goal shared by most people.
✗ In this essay I will tell about happiness.
✓ This essay examines / argues that …
✗ The happiness is important for the people.
✓ Happiness is important for people.
✗ This essay discusses about well-being.
✓ This essay discusses well-being.
✗ In this essay will be discussed happiness.
✓ This essay discusses happiness.
✗ It will be argued happiness and money.
✓ It will be argued that money matters less than health.
✗ fulfilment … fulfill (two spellings in one essay)
✓ British: fulfil, fulfilment — choose one and keep it.

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own introduction.

CriterionA C1 introduction …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear position from the foundation to the floor guide
O · Organisationhas one idea per sentence (general → background → focus → thesis → roadmap) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: thesis and roadmap structures (It will be argued that …, While …, this essay contends that …, It first examines …, then considers …)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students wrote an introduction for the Level 2 task (A meaningful job is more important than a high salary …). Mark both. (Sample texts written for this book.)

Student A
Choosing a job is one of the biggest decisions in a person’s life. Many young people today must choose between a high salary and a job which they find interesting. In this essay, a meaningful job is a job that is useful. It will be argued that meaningful job more important than salary, because money is not give happiness for long time. The essay first examine the salary, then it considering the meaning of work and finally the conclusion.
Student B
Few decisions shape adult life as strongly as the choice of a career. For many graduates, this choice now involves a difficult trade-off between a well-paid post and work that feels genuinely worthwhile. Here, a meaningful job is taken to mean one that uses a person’s abilities and benefits others. While an adequate salary is essential for security, this essay contends that meaning contributes more to long-term well-being. It first examines the limits of income, then considers the sources of fulfilment at work, and finally discusses how young people might balance the two.

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: scan the text for names in front of brackets — (2019), (2021) … How many different sources does the writer use?

Talent or Effort? What Really Builds Success

An academic essay with sources · about 500 words · C1 · written for this book · the four cited sources are fictional

AWhen a young chess player from Tashkent wins an international tournament, or a student from a small village earns a place at a leading university, people often reach for the same word: talent. The explanation is attractive because it is simple, and because it seems to excuse the rest of us. However, researchers who study expertise increasingly question whether natural ability alone can account for outstanding achievement. This essay argues that sustained, well-guided effort explains success more convincingly than innate talent, although neither talent nor circumstances can be ignored.

BThe strongest argument for effort comes from research on how experts develop. According to Rashidova (2019), people who reach the highest levels in music, sport and science have usually spent many years on deliberate practice: focused training that targets their weaknesses rather than repeating what they already do well. Crucially, she notes that such practice is “rarely enjoyable and almost never accidental” (p. 47). If this is correct, much of what observers call talent may be the visible result of years of invisible work. A pianist’s effortless performance, in other words, is effortless only on the night of the concert. Effort, not a mysterious gift, is what the audience is really applauding.

CA second argument concerns beliefs about ability. Tursunov and Lee (2021) found that university students who saw intelligence as something that can grow were more likely to keep trying after a poor result than students who saw it as fixed. As the authors point out, a single failure means very different things to these two groups: for the first, it is information; for the second, it is a verdict. This suggests that the story people tell themselves about talent can shape the effort they are prepared to invest. However, the study was conducted at only two universities, so its conclusions may not apply to every context.

DThis is not to say that innate differences do not exist. Halimova (2018) acknowledges that physical characteristics such as height matter in some sports, and that children differ in how quickly they acquire certain skills. Yet she also stresses that early advantages tend to grow only when they are noticed and cultivated: “A gift that nobody waters rarely becomes a garden” (Halimova, 2018, p. 112). Talent, on this view, is better understood as a head start than as a guarantee.

Who is speaking — the writer or a source? Watch the stamps.

☆More practice · Quick check on A–D

1. Which word do people “reach for” in A?

2. What does deliberate practice target (B)?

3. How many universities were in the study (C)?

4. What does a gift need before it grows (D)?

Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 4 · Practical class 32
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

EFinally, any honest account of success must consider circumstances. Okafor (2020) argues that access to good teachers, equipment and free time is unevenly distributed, and that what looks like individual effort is often supported by family and community. In Uzbekistan, for example, many successful athletes and musicians speak about the role of a single dedicated coach or teacher in their town or mahalla. Effort, then, does not happen in a vacuum; it needs opportunities in which to grow.

FIn conclusion, the evidence reviewed here suggests that success is built rather than born. Talent may open the door and circumstances may decide how wide it opens, but it is long-term, deliberate effort that carries a person through it.

References (fictional sources, written for this book)
Halimova, N. (2018). Gifts and gardens: How early ability grows. Minaret Press.
Okafor, C. (2020). Opportunity and the myth of the self-made achiever. Caravan Review of Social Science, 14(1), 22–39.
Rashidova, D. (2019). The making of experts: Practice, patience and performance. Silk Road Academic Books.
Tursunov, A., & Lee, J. (2021). Fixed or growing? Students’ beliefs about ability. Journal of Learning on the Silk Road, 8(2), 115–131.

Real sources of two terms: deliberate practice (K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues) and growth mindset (Carol S. Dweck).
Dweck, C. S. (2006). Mindset: The new psychology of success. Random House.
Ericsson, K. A., Krampe, R. T., & Tesch-Römer, C. (1993). The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance. Psychological Review, 100(3), 363–406.

Four ways to lay a source rule
PatternExample
Author firstOkafor (2020) argues that … · Tursunov and Lee (2021) found that …
Information first… is unevenly distributed (Okafor, 2020). · … (Tursunov & Lee, 2021).
Signal phraseAccording to Rashidova (2019), … · As Halimova (2018) points out, …
QuotationRashidova (2019) calls it “rarely enjoyable” (p. 47). · “…” (Halimova, 2018, p. 112).

Choose the verb: found · showed (a study’s evidence) · argues · claims (a position) · suggests (careful) · notes · points out (neutral) · acknowledges (accepts a point against) · questions (doubts)

Three rules

  • No double subject: According to Okafor, she argues … ✗ → According to Okafor (2020), access … ✓
  • As X notes, + clause — no that: As Halimova notes that … ✗ → As Halimova notes, … ✓
  • Tense (as in Stop 23): one study → past (found) · an author’s view → present (argues) · the state of the field → present perfect (Several studies have shown …). “and” or “&”: “and” in your sentence, “&” in brackets.
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. According to Rashidova, she says practice matters.
2. As Okafor points out that chances are unequal.
3. Halimova (2018) says about talent that it grows.
4. … beliefs shape effort (Tursunov and Lee, 2021).

Level up: stance and evaluation

CONTINUED

At C1 you do not only report a source. You show where the author stands, make each finding no stronger than its evidence and judge the source.

ToolPhrasesExample
Stance verbs
show the author’s position		contends · maintains · concedes · demonstrates · casts doubt onOkafor (2020) contends that individual effort is often supported by the community.
Research hedging
a finding, no stronger than the evidence		suggests · appears to · is likely to · there is some evidence thatBeliefs about ability appear to shape how long students keep trying.
Evaluation
judge a source’s strength and limits		a key strength of … · is limited by · relies onTursunov and Lee’s study is limited by its focus on two universities.
Nominalisation
verb → noun		find → finding · limit → limitation · acknowledge → acknowledgementHalimova’s acknowledgement that height matters makes her argument more balanced.

The Blueprint: the bricks of the shaft

10 MIN

Above the door rises the shaft of the minaret. Its decorative bands are your body paragraphs. Each band is laid in four courses, and the bricks borrowed from other builders carry their maker’s stamp: the citation.

Without the Comment course, a paragraph is only a list of sources.

CourseWhat goes insideExample from paragraph CWords
1 · Claimone point that supports the thesisA second argument concerns beliefs about ability.≈ 15
2 · Citeevidence from a source + (Author, year)Tursunov and Lee (2021) found that … As the authors point out, …≈ 50
3 · Commentyour voice: what it means, how strong it isThis suggests that … However, the study was conducted at only two universities …≈ 50
4 · Connectback to the thesis (or on to the next band)missing in C. Write one: ≈ 20

The stamp has two parts: a short one in the text, (Author, year), and a full one in the reference list at the end.

Source A · a fictional journal article

Nazarova, M. (2020). Late starters: Adult learners and the power of practice. Caravan Journal of Language Learning, 6(3), 45–60.

p. 51 “Adults who practise for a short time every day often overtake younger learners who practise rarely.”

Source B · a fictional book

p. 9 “Learners with a good ear for sounds master pronunciation faster at first, but this advantage becomes smaller over time.”

Task: Natural talent is more important than hard work in learning a foreign language. To what extent do you agree? Here is one body paragraph, written for this book.
1 · Claim
(1) The main reason why effort matters more than talent in language learning is that regular practice can make up for a late or slow start.
2 · Cite
(2) Nazarova (2020) found that brief but daily practice often allowed adult learners to move ahead of younger ones who practised only occasionally. (3) Petrov and Azimova (2022) acknowledge that learners with “a good ear for sounds” have an early lead in pronunciation, but they add that the lead “becomes smaller over time” (p. 9).
3 · Comment
(4) This suggests that talent may decide how fast a learner starts, but not how far he or she goes. (5) It should be noted, however, that both sources focus mainly on speaking, so the picture may be different for academic writing.
4 · Connect
(6) Steady effort, therefore, rather than a gifted ear, is what most language learners can rely on.
References
Nazarova, M. (2020). Late starters: Adult learners and the power of practice. Caravan Journal of Language Learning, 6(3), 45–60.
Petrov, I., & Azimova, S. (2022). The musical ear: Sound, memory and language. Minaret Press.

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own paragraph.

CriterionA C1 paragraph …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear position from the claim to the connect course
O · Organisationhas one idea per paragraph (Claim · Cite · Comment · Connect) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: citation patterns and reporting tenses (According to X (year), … · X (year) found … · X (year) argues … · As X notes, …)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students wrote a body paragraph for the model task (Natural talent is more important than hard work in learning a foreign language …) with Sources A and B. Mark both. (Sample texts written for this book.)

Student A
Hard work is more important than talent for learning a language. According to Nazarova (2020), adults who study a little every day often do better than younger learners who rarely study. Petrov and Azimova (2022) says that a good ear is helpful, but only at the beginning. Also, many people on the internet think that talent is not so important. There are many good students in our group who are not talented.
Student B
A further reason to favour effort is that the advantage of a good ear appears to be temporary. Petrov and Azimova (2022) concede that such learners have an early lead in pronunciation, yet they maintain that this benefit “becomes smaller over time” (p. 9). Nazarova’s (2020) finding that short daily practice helped adults to move ahead of younger learners points in the same direction. Although both sources focus on speaking, they suggest that persistence, rather than an innate ear, determines how far most learners progress.

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

☆ Make it C1 (model answers): 1 Rashidova (2019) maintains that deliberate practice matters most. · 2 Beliefs about ability appear to change the effort students make. · 3 The study is limited by its focus on two universities. · 4 Halimova (2018) concedes that talent exists but stresses that it must be cultivated. · 5 Tursunov and Lee’s (2021) finding that beliefs matter is important.

5 · Blueprint and model paragraph

Connect for C (model): Effort, it seems, depends partly on what people believe about talent.
Need a citation: sentences 1 and 4.
1 found · acknowledge · add; acknowledge accepts a point against. · 2 (3) copies exact words → quotation marks + page; (2) is a real paraphrase: new structure, new words, same meaning (page optional). · 3 sentence (5). · 4 Brief but daily practice often allowed adult learners to move ahead of younger ones (Nazarova, 2020). · 5 (Petrov & Azimova, 2022). · 6 the thesis. · ☆ 7 e.g. Petrov and Azimova (2022) concede that … · The evidence is limited by its focus on speaking.

6 · Hearsay (model answers)

2 Tursunov and Lee (2021) found that students who believed their ability was fixed tended to give up more easily after a low mark. · 3 Halimova (2018) accepts that tall players have an advantage in some sports, but she argues that such early gifts grow only with care and training. · 4 Okafor (2020) argues that not every child has the same chance to work with good teachers or to find free time for training.

7 · Writing ladder (model)

Level 1: One important reason why effort matters is that students’ beliefs about ability shape how hard they try. Tursunov and Lee (2021) found that students who believed that intelligence can be developed were more likely to persist after a disappointing result. As the authors point out, a single failure can be useful feedback for one group but a final judgement for the other. This suggests that effort depends partly on beliefs. However, the study covered only two universities. Therefore, teaching that ability can grow may help students succeed.

8 · Be the examiner (suggested)

Student A: T 2 · O 1 · V 2 · G 2 (T: ends with an anecdote; O: no Comment or Connect — a list joined by Also; V: helpful, good students; G: Petrov and Azimova … says). Student B: 3 · 3 · 3 · 3. The biggest difference is in O (2 points).
☆ Be the editor: e.g. Petrov and Azimova (2022) say that … + a Comment sentence.

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: read the thesis (the last two sentences of A) and then paragraph F. Does the lantern match the door? yes   no   partly

Free to Choose, Responsible for the Choice

An academic essay · Society and ethics · about 510 words · C1 · written for this book

AFreedom is one of the most valued ideas of the modern world: it is written into constitutions, celebrated in songs and demanded in protests. Yet almost every freedom people enjoy has limits. A driver is free to travel, but not at any speed; a citizen may speak freely, but not to spread false accusations about a neighbour. This essay argues that freedom and responsibility are not opposites but partners, because liberty can only last when people accept responsibility for how they use it. It examines personal choices, freedom of speech and the role of the community in turn.

BAt the personal level, freedom means autonomy: the right to make decisions about one’s own life. Choosing a profession, a partner or a way of life without pressure is, for many people, the heart of a free existence. However, choices rarely affect only the person who makes them. A student who decides to miss classes for a month also affects the group project that depends on her, and a smoker in a shared stairwell imposes his choice on his neighbours. Autonomy, in other words, comes with an obligation to consider others.

CThe same principle applies to speech. The ability to express opinions, to criticise those in power and to share information is widely seen as essential to a healthy society, and social media has extended this freedom to almost anyone with a phone. At the same time, it has made careless words more dangerous: a false rumour can now travel across a country in a few hours. Many legal systems therefore protect free expression while placing constraints on defamation, threats and incitement to violence. Such limits are not the enemy of free speech; they are what allow many voices to be heard safely.

DCommunities, finally, play a central role in balancing rights and duties. In the Uzbek mahalla, for example, neighbours often agree on informal rules about noise late at night, the use of shared courtyards or help for families in need. Nobody signs these rules, yet most residents uphold them, because they understand that the comfort of each household depends on the cooperation of all. This collective sense of responsibility is not a restriction imposed from above but an agreement that protects everyone’s freedom.

ECritics might reply that the language of responsibility is easily misused: governments or powerful groups can restrict liberty “for the common good” when they simply wish to silence opponents. This danger is real. It suggests, however, not that responsibility should be rejected, but that any limits on freedom should themselves be accountable: clearly explained, fairly applied and open to public discussion.

Read A, then F. Which words come back?

Language toolkit: concluding language

10 MIN

A conclusion does three jobs: it looks back, weighs up and looks ahead.

Notice find it

Find these phrases in the text and complete them.

1. (F) In conclusion, this essay that freedom and responsibility depend …

2. (F) … liberty survives when people consider how their choices affect others …

3. (F) the real measure of a free society is not how few rules it has …

4. (E) This danger is .

5. (E) It suggests, , not that responsibility should be rejected, but that …

6. (C) Such limits are the enemy of free speech; they are what allow …

Three jobs, three kinds of language rule
JobLanguageExample
SignalIn conclusion, · To conclude, · Overall, · Taken together, …Overall, …
Look backThis essay has argued / shown that … · As has been shown, …This essay has shown that …
Weigh upOn balance, … · To a large extent, … · The evidence partly suggests …On balance, the benefits win.
Look aheadPerhaps … · If …, … may … · … should therefore … · It remains to be seen whether …If rules are fair, people may keep them.

Three rules

  • Look back with the present perfect: This essay has argued … ✓ · This essay will argue … ✗
  • One signal is enough: In conclusion, to sum up, … ✗ · In conclusion, … ✓
  • Weigh precisely: on balance · to a large extent · partly ✓ · 100% · it is totally proved ✗
Fix it correct
Broken sentence (all from conclusions)Fixed sentence

Level up: synthesis and closure

CONTINUED

At C1 a conclusion does not list the body again. It pulls the ideas into one, weighs them with care and closes with a claim that is wider than the thesis but still careful.

ToolPhrasesExample
Synthesis
join the bands in one sentence		Taken together, … · Whether in …, … or …, … · What emerges is …Whether in personal life, speech or the mahalla, liberty depends on responsibility.
Nominalisation
verb or adjective → noun		protect → protection · accept → acceptance · willing → willingnessPeople accept duties willingly. → The willing acceptance of duties keeps freedom alive.
Concessive closure
admit, then hold your line		While …, … · Although … may …, … · Granted, …; even so, …While some limits are misused, fair and open rules protect liberty.
Hedged final thought
look further, carefully		Perhaps … · may well · It remains to be seen whether …Clear online rules may well make social media freer, not less free.

The Blueprint: the lantern on top

At the top of a great minaret sits the lantern, a ring of arched windows under a small dome. From there you can see every part of the building below — and far beyond it. Your conclusion does the same.

The conclusion keeps the thesis of the introduction, in new words and with a wider view.

LanternConclusionWhat goes insideWords
CorniceRestated thesisthe door’s claim in new words + a signal≈ 20
WindowsSummary + evaluationa short line per band; then weigh them up≈ 30–40
Dome + lightFinal thoughtso what? meaning, advice, prediction or question≈ 20–30
No new bricks—no new arguments, examples, statistics or sources0

Coherence = the ideas fit together: the lantern sits on this shaft, not on another building. Cohesion = the words hold together: echoes of key words, synonyms (freedom → liberty), reference words (this, such) and linkers.

Student A
In conclusion, this essay has argued that students can use AI tools, but they must be responsible for their work. AI tools help students to plan and edit faster, but copying are dangerous for learning. Also, a survey in my university shows that most students use chatbots every day. Thank you for your attention.
Student B
Taken together, the arguments considered here suggest that students should be free to use AI tools, provided that they remain accountable for every word they submit. Such tools undeniably make planning and editing more efficient; copying their output without understanding it, however, undermines both learning and honesty. On balance, clear university rules can turn this freedom into a responsible habit. Ultimately, the real question may be not whether students use AI, but whether they still think for themselves.

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: skim A and G. Where does the writer locate the main causes of stress?
in students’ personalities   in the way student life is organised   in social media

Where Stress Comes From

A review essay · about 540 words · C1 · written for this book

AAsk any group of second-year students how they feel during the exam session, and the answers are rarely calm. Stress is not new to university life; a certain amount of pressure can sharpen attention and push people to prepare. The concern among educators is different: for a growing number of students, stress seems to have become constant rather than occasional. Before universities can respond sensibly, they need to understand where this pressure comes from.

BThe most visible source is academic workload. Many students take several courses with overlapping deadlines, and assessment is often concentrated in a few intense weeks. Owing to this, students tend to study in long, irregular bursts rather than steadily. Consequently, tiredness accumulates, and small setbacks — a missed deadline, a disappointing mark — begin to feel like disasters. Pressure, in other words, does not simply add up; it multiplies.

CMoney is a second, quieter contributing factor. In Uzbekistan, as in many countries, numerous students pay tuition fees under a contract, and many live away from home in rented flats or dormitories. Some take part-time jobs in cafés or call centres to cover their costs. Work in itself is not harmful; it can build skills and confidence. When working hours collide with lectures and revision, however, the result is less sleep, less study time and a permanent feeling of being behind.

DExpectations form a third layer. Families often make real sacrifices to send a son or daughter to university, and students are well aware of this. The wish to repay that trust can motivate, but it can also turn every exam into a test of loyalty. Comparison adds to the weight: online, classmates seem to win scholarships and internships effortlessly, while one’s own difficulties stay invisible. Social media use and stress are clearly linked, yet researchers still debate which way the influence runs: stressed students may simply spend more time online.

EThese causes rarely act alone. A heavy workload leads to late nights, and late nights result in sleep deprivation. Poor sleep, in turn, weakens concentration, which produces weaker results — and weaker results exacerbate worries about money and family expectations. This chain explains why stress can grow so quickly once it starts, and why a single measure, such as a longer exam timetable, may bring only limited relief.

FThe effects are felt both inside and outside the classroom. Many studies suggest that prolonged stress is associated with headaches, poor sleep and problems with memory, all of which are detrimental to learning. Students under constant pressure may skip meals, withdraw into social isolation or lose interest in subjects they once enjoyed. In serious cases, stress can give rise to anxiety disorders or burnout that require professional help. Paradoxically, the students who work hardest to succeed may be the ones most at risk.

GNone of this means that pressure should be removed from university life. Challenge is part of learning, and many students cope with it well, especially when they have strong friendships and know where to ask for help; such support builds resilience. What it does suggest is that stress stems less from personal weakness than from the way study, money and expectations are organised. If the causes are structural, at least part of the response must be structural too.

Find the chain: in which paragraph does one effect become the next cause?

Language toolkit: cause and effect

10 MIN

These structures link a cause to its effect, or an effect back to its cause.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the review essay and complete them.

1. (B) this, students tend to study in long, irregular bursts …

2. (B) , tiredness accumulates …

3. (E) A heavy workload late nights, and late nights sleep deprivation.

4. (F) … stress can anxiety disorders or burnout …

5. (G) … stress less from personal weakness than from the way study … are organised.

Five kinds of channel rule
ChannelGrammarExample
because / since / as+ subject + verbWe sleep less because we work late.
because of / owing to / due to+ noun phraseOwing to late work, we sleep less.
Consequently, · As a result, · Hence,new sentenceDates clash. Consequently, we panic.
lead to · result in · give rise tocause → effectDeadlines result in late nights.
stem from · result from · arise fromeffect ← causeAnxiety often stems from debt.

Four rules

  • Mind the direction: X results in Y (→)  ·  Y results from X (←). Never is resulted from.
  • Owing to / due to + noun: owing to long hours ✓  ·  owing to they work long hours ✗
  • Consequently starts a sentence: … clash. Consequently, … ✓  ·  clash, consequently ✗
  • Lead + person + to: stress leads students to skip meals ✓  ·  leads to students skip ✗
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. Owing to students work at night, they miss lectures.
2. Much stress is resulted from overlapping deadlines.
3. Exams start in May, consequently students panic.
4. Isolation can lead to students feel anxious.
5. The reason of student stress is the workload.

Level up: causal verbs and careful causes

CONTINUED

At C1 you name a cause precisely, you pack it into a noun phrase, and you never claim more than the evidence shows: being linked is not the same as causing.

ToolPhrasesExample
Causal verbs
more precise than “cause”		trigger · fuel · contribute to · precipitate · compoundOverlapping deadlines trigger panic in the last week of term.
Nominalised causes
the cause as a noun phrase		the rise in · the lack of · the accumulation of · the pressure toThe rise in rent has led many students to take evening jobs.
Careful causation
linked ≠ caused		is associated with · is linked to · appears to · is likely toHeavy phone use is associated with shorter sleep.
Result chains
one effect becomes a cause		thereby + -ing · which in turn · a vicious circleStudents work late, thereby reducing the time left for sleep.

The Blueprint: build an ariq system

10 MIN

A cause-and-effect essay explains why something happens, what it leads to, or both — and proves each link with evidence. Typical tasks: What are the causes of …? · What effects does … have? · Discuss the causes and effects of …

Every cause in the thesis map needs its own channel, and every channel must lead to an effect.

Part of the systemPart of the essayWhat goes insideWords
HeadworksIntroductionHook → the issue and why it matters → thesis map: the causes and/or effects you will trace≈ 60
Channel 1Body 1 · cause 1Factor · Link (how it works) · Offer evidence · Where it leads≈ 70
Channel 2Body 2 · cause 2F · L · O · W again, with the second cause≈ 60
FieldsBody 3 · effectsTwo or three effects + one chain (… which in turn …)≈ 50
Mirob’s reportConclusionThe whole system in new words + what should change at the source≈ 40

Layout A · Block

All the causes first (one channel each), then the effects in the fields. Best when the causes are separate: workload, money, expectations.

Layout B · Chain

One link per paragraph: A → B → C → D. Best when each effect becomes the next cause: late nights → poor sleep → weak marks.

Which tasks ask for a cause-and-effect essay? Tick two.

Should universities replace exams with coursework? Discuss both views and give your opinion.
Many students feel exhausted by the end of the first year. Why is this, and how does it affect their studies?
Exam stress is a serious problem. What can universities do to reduce it?
What effects does moving to the capital have on young people from the regions?
Is it better to study in your home town or abroad? Give your opinion.

Walk through the system

CONTINUED
Task: Stress has become a common part of student life. What are the main causes of stress among university students, and what effects does it have? Class model · about 300 words (your MT10 essay is longer: 2–3 pages) · written for this book
Headworks
HOOKFor many young people, the first year at university is the beginning of freedom; for a surprising number, it is also the beginning of chronic stress. ISSUEStudent stress is often treated as an individual weakness rather than as the predictable outcome of identifiable conditions. THESIS MAPThis essay argues that it stems largely from the sudden demand for independent study and from uncertainty about future employment, and that its effects reach well beyond exam results.
Channel 1
(1) The first contributing factor is the abrupt transition from school to university. (2) At school, revision is largely organised by teachers; at university, students must plan their own reading and meet several deadlines at once. (3) A student who moves from a district town to Tashkent, for instance, may have to manage rent and cooking for the first time during the first exam session. (4) Owing to this sudden accumulation of responsibilities, many first-year students fall behind early, and the gap then feeds further anxiety.
Channel 2
A second source of pressure is uncertainty about the future. Student surveys in many countries list future employment among young people’s main worries [source needed], and many students therefore collect certificates and internships alongside their degree. Consequently, free time shrinks, and every low mark seems to threaten a whole career.
Fields
These pressures give rise to physical and academic effects. Students under strain frequently sacrifice sleep, and sleep deprivation, in turn, is detrimental to memory and concentration. As a result, a vicious circle may develop: stress lowers performance, and lower performance increases stress.
Mirob’s report
In conclusion, student stress is not simply a matter of character: it results from the demands of independent study and from uncertainty about the future, and it damages both health and learning. Universities should therefore work at the source, for example by teaching study skills in the first semester.
“[source needed]” marks a claim that needs a real author and year in your own essay.

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own essay.

CriterionA C1 essay …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear position from the headworks to the mirob’s report
O · Organisationhas one idea per paragraph (F.L.O.W.) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students wrote Channel 1 for the Levels 1–2 task (Many first-year students feel lonely …). Mark both.

Student A
The first cause of loneliness is moving far away from family and old friends. Due to students live in a new city, they have nobody to talk to after lectures. For example, a student from Termez may spend every weekend alone in the dormitory. This isolation is resulted from the move, and it can lead to students skip seminars, so their marks become lower.
Student B
The first contributing factor is the sudden loss of a familiar support network. Students who move to Tashkent from the regions leave behind family and school friends, and they tend to find it hard to form new ties while adjusting to an unfamiliar workload. A typical case is a student who spends weekends alone in a rented flat while classmates go home. Such isolation is associated with lower motivation, which in turn may lead students to skip the very seminars where friendships could begin.

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: look at paragraphs A and G only. What will the writer recommend?
banning buffets   one strict rule   a combination of treatments

Too Good to Waste: A Diagnosis

A feature article with sources · about 550 words · C1 · written for this book · UNEP (2024) is a real report; the other three sources are fictional.

APicture the morning after a wedding: trays of plov, half-eaten salads and whole loaves of bread are carried out of the hall. One meal thrown away seems a small matter; repeated in millions of homes, canteens and shops, it becomes one of the largest leaks in the world’s food system. According to the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP, 2024), about 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted in 2022 — roughly a fifth of the food available to consumers.

BDefining the problem is less simple than it seems. Some loss is unavoidable: bones, peel and shells were never meant to be eaten. The real concern is edible food that is discarded, because it wastes the water, land and labour used to produce it. Nor is this only a problem of rich countries: UNEP (2024) found that average household waste differs surprisingly little between high-income and lower-middle-income countries.

CThe causes lie partly in how food is sold. Special offers can persuade shoppers to buy more than they can eat, and perishable goods such as bread, fruit and dairy products spoil quickly. Partly, however, the causes lie in custom. At celebrations, hosts may cook far more than guests can eat, because an empty dish can feel like a sign of poor hospitality. In a survey of one university canteen, Nematova (2023) found that most of the discarded food came from portions that were simply too large. Treating only the bins would be like treating a fever without asking what caused it.

DThe most common prescription is personal: planning meals, writing a shopping list and eating leftovers. Such measures are cheap and immediately available. Their weakness is that they rely on good intentions, which busy people tend to forget. Ferrari and Qosimova (2022) found that families who kept a shopping list for a month threw away less food, but most stopped once the study ended. It is advisable, therefore, to combine personal habits with changes in the environment.

EInstitutions can play a part as well. Canteens can offer half portions, serve bread on request and measure what is left on plates. These interventions are feasible, cost little and send a clear signal that food matters, but a strict rule on portion sizes may annoy customers and simply move the waste to the dormitory kitchen. A more promising approach would be to involve students in designing the changes, so that they are owned rather than imposed.

FThe most ambitious solution targets the surplus itself: passing it on before it is wasted. Food banks and sharing networks collect unsold but safe food from shops and give it to people in need, and in many mahallas, as Sharipov (2021) argues, neighbours have long shared what remains after a celebration. Such schemes could reach thousands of families; however, they require storage, transport and clear food-safety rules, which are slow and costly to organise.

GNo single treatment is likely to cure the problem. Personal habits work quickly but fade; canteen rules are practical but may be resented; redistribution is powerful but demanding. It would therefore be wise to treat food waste like a chronic condition: with a combination of measures, regular check-ups and patience. The aim should not be to make people feel guilty about every crumb, but to make sure that good food feeds people, not rubbish bins.

References (Ferrari & Qosimova, Nematova and Sharipov are fictional, written for this book)
Ferrari, L., & Qosimova, M. (2022). Lists, leftovers and good intentions: A one-month study of household food planning. Caravan Journal of Consumer Studies, 7(2), 41–58.
Nematova, D. (2023). What students leave on the plate: Food waste in a university canteen. Oasis Review of Public Health, 5(1), 12–27.
Sharipov, B. (2021). Sharing the dasturxon: Food, neighbours and the mahalla. Minaret Press.
United Nations Environment Programme. (2024). Food waste index report 2024. Think Eat Save: Tracking progress to halve global food waste. https://wedocs.unep.org/20.500.11822/45230

Walk through the tabib’s room

CONTINUED
Task: In many university canteens, large amounts of edible food are thrown away every day. Analyse the problem and evaluate possible solutions. · Class model · about 300 words (your MT10 essay is longer: 2–3 pages) · written for this book
Door · symptoms
HOOKAt lunchtime, a university canteen feeds hundreds of students; by two o’clock, its bins are full of rice, soup and bread. PROBLEMThe difficulty is not leftovers as such, but edible food that is discarded every day, although it has cost money, water and labour to produce. THESISThis essay argues that the problem has two root causes — portions that are fixed and too large, and waste that nobody measures — and that it can be reduced by flexible portions and by making the waste visible.
Desk · diagnosis
It is tempting to blame careless students, but the diagnosis is not so simple. Most canteens serve one standard portion, whatever the student’s appetite. At the same time, the waste disappears into the bins unseen, so neither the cooks nor the students know how much is lost. Consequently, the same amount is wasted day after day.
Jar 1
(1) The first treatment should therefore target the portions themselves. (2) If canteens offered half portions and served bread on request, students would take only what they intended to eat. (3) In a survey of one canteen, Nematova (2023) found that most discarded food came from portions that were too large. (4) The main drawback is that canteen income may fall; however, this could be mitigated by pricing half portions fairly.
Jar 2
A second, complementary treatment is a weekly “waste board” showing how many kilograms were thrown away. This addresses the invisibility of the problem. Its limitation is that numbers alone rarely change habits, so it is advisable that the board be designed with the student council.
Prescription
In conclusion, flexible portions should come first, because they lie within the canteen’s control; the waste board would then help students change their habits. As any tabib would insist, weighing the bins at the start and end of the semester would show whether the treatment works.
References
Nematova, D. (2023). What students leave on the plate: Food waste in a university canteen. Oasis Review of Public Health, 5(1), 12–27. (fictional)

I recommend hosts to count the guests and to cook for this number. It must to be easy for families, but some hosts may not like it. We suggest to give the leftovers to neighbours. This is the best solution of this problem.
Student B
The first treatment should target the custom of cooking for far more guests than are invited. Were hosts to plan for the confirmed number of guests plus a small reserve, far less plov would be left. Sharipov (2021) describes mahallas where such planning is combined with sharing the surplus. While this measure is cost-effective and feasible, its main drawback is that hosts may fear appearing ungenerous; this could be mitigated if respected elders set the example.

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: count the sources. How many different sources does the writer cite?

Fictional sources. Every author, journal, publisher, website and DOI in this lesson was invented for teaching. Do not search for them, and never invent sources in your own work.

Silent Losses in the Drylands

A short literature review · about 500 words · C1 · written for this book · the reference list follows the text

ABiodiversity loss is usually pictured in rainforests or coral reefs, yet some of the quietest losses are taking place in drylands. The deserts, steppes and river valleys of Central Asia are home to endemic species found nowhere else, and many of them depend on habitats that are shrinking (Karimova & Holt, 2021). This short review summarises what recent studies say about the causes of decline and about possible responses, and notes where the evidence is still weak.

BMost authors agree that the main driver is habitat loss. Along the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, tugai forests — dense riverside woodlands of poplar, willow and tamarisk — have retreated as water has been diverted for agriculture (Nazarov, 2019). Because these forests shelter birds, mammals and insects that cannot survive in the open desert, their decline affects whole communities of species rather than single animals. In the lower reaches of the Amu Darya, the drying of lakes and wetlands has also taken away resting places for migrating birds (Nazarov, 2019).

CA second pressure is the spread of invasive species. Lindqvist et al. (2022) describe how plants introduced along roads and canals can outcompete native shrubs, especially where the soil has already been disturbed. As they put it, “invasions rarely begin in healthy ecosystems; they begin where people have already opened the door” (p. 47). Climate change may add to these pressures: hotter summers and less predictable rain are expected to make dryland species more vulnerable, although the evidence for individual species is still limited (Karimova & Holt, 2021).

DPollinators deserve particular attention. Wild bees and other insects pollinate many crops, from fruit trees to melons, as well as wild plants, yet they receive far less research attention than large mammals. Rahimov (2020) argues that the monitoring of insect populations in the region remains patchy, which makes it difficult to say how fast they are declining. Most records, he adds, come from a few sites near cities, while remote mountain and desert areas are hardly studied. Without such data, conservation priorities may be set by what is visible rather than by what is important.

EThe literature also points to responses. Protected areas along rivers can preserve fragments of habitat, but Nazarov (2019) warns that a reserve without water is “a fence around a memory” (p. 112). Community-based approaches, in which local farmers help to manage pastures and water, have shown promising results in several projects (Green Valley Trust, 2023). Seed banks and tree nurseries offer a further safety net, although they cannot replace living habitats (Karimova & Holt, 2021). However, as Lindqvist et al. (2022) point out, most projects are short, and long-term evaluations are rare.

FTaken together, these sources suggest that dryland biodiversity is threatened less by a single dramatic event than by many slow changes acting together. Above all, they indicate that protecting species in a dry land means protecting its water. They also reveal a gap: local, long-term data are scarce. For students who wish to research the topic, this gap is an invitation.

Which in-text citations point to the same source in the list?
Jigsaw option. Groups take A–B, C–D or E–F, find their citations in the reference list and teach a mixed group in 60 seconds.
☆Talk after reading: For a claim about wild bees in Uzbekistan, would you trust a journal article, a charity web page or a video most? Why?

Language toolkit: citing accurately

10 MIN
Remember from Stop 23: the APA 7 call slips — (Karimova & Holt, 2021) · (Lindqvist et al., 2022) · (Nazarov, 2019, p. 112) — and the parts of a reference: Who → When → What → Where. When you write a reference, look back at Read the card. This stop adds accuracy: exact words, the right page, the same meaning.
Notice find it

Find these in the review.

1. (C) How does the reader know which words are exactly Lindqvist et al.’s?

2. (E) The page of Nazarov’s quotation: Why does a quotation need a page?

3. (C) A hedge that the writer kept from the source:

Four rules of accurate citing rule
Rule✓ Accurate✗ Inaccurate
1 · Exact words → “ ” + pageNazarov (2019) calls such a reserve “a fence around a memory” (p. 112).… calls such a reserve a fence around a memory (Nazarov, 2019). — copied words without marks
2 · Shorten a quotation with …, but keep its meaning“invasions rarely begin in healthy ecosystems …” (Lindqvist et al., 2022, p. 47)“invasions … begin in healthy ecosystems” — the meaning is reversed
3 · Paraphrase: new words, same meaning, same strengthHotter summers are expected to make dryland species more vulnerable (Karimova & Holt, 2021).Climate change will destroy dryland species (Karimova & Holt, 2021). — may became will
4 · Record as you read: author, year, page; Q · P · MQ “a fence around a memory” — Nazarov, 2019, p. 112reserves need water!! — no source, no page

Reporting tenses (the Stop 23 rule): one study → past simple (Lindqvist et al. (2022) found …) · an author’s view → present simple (Rahimov (2020) argues …) · the state of the field → present perfect (Several projects have shown …).

Fix it correct
Inaccurate sentence (ONE mistake each)Corrected
1. Nazarov (2019) writes that a reserve without water is a fence around a memory (p. 112).
2. “Invasions rarely begin in healthy ecosystems” (Lindqvist et al., 2022).
3. As Nazarov (2019) warns, a reserve without water is “a fence around memory” (p. 112).
4. Rahimov (2020) found that insect monitoring in the region remains patchy.
5. Community projects have been successful everywhere (Green Valley Trust, 2023).

Level up: reporting and judging a source

CONTINUED

A C1 annotation does more than say what a source is “about”. It reports the authors’ move precisely, reports results no more strongly than the evidence allows and judges the source in specific terms.

ToolPhrasesExample
Precise reporting verbs
what the authors do		examine · investigate · contend · synthesise · concludeRahimov contends that insect monitoring in the region is patchy.
Research hedging
results, not stronger than the data		the findings suggest · appear to · may not be generalisableThe findings may not be generalisable beyond one valley.
Specific evaluation
strength + limit, never “interesting”		a notable strength is · is limited by · offers a useful frameworkThe review offers a useful framework for grouping threats.
Nominalisation
verb → noun		analyse → analysis · find → findings · conclude → conclusionTheir analysis of sixty studies maps a large field.

The Blueprint: the library shelf

10 MIN

An annotated bibliography is a list of sources, each with a full reference (the label) and a short annotation (the catalogue card) that describes the source, judges it and says how you will use it.

The reference tells a reader where to find the source; the annotation tells them whether it is worth reading.

Part of the libraryIn the bibliographyWhat goes inside
The shelfthe whole listA → Z by first author’s surname · hanging indent · APA 7 all the way
The labelthe referenceWho · When · What · Where (+ DOI) — complete and accurate
The card · CContentthe aim and the main argument or findings (1–2 sentences)
The card · AApproachwhat kind of source it is and how the authors found out (review? survey? field study?)
The card · RReliabilitya real strength + a real limit (peer review, date, place, sample)
The card · DDestinationhow you will use it: which part of your project, for which point
Compare it think
The catalogue · Stop 23The stamp · Stop 32The shelf · Stop 36
Your rolea reader who follows a citation to its carda writer who stamps each borrowed bricka writer who records and judges a whole source
You makea citation mapa body paragraph with citationsan annotated bibliography
Accuracy checkDoes every call slip have a card?Is every borrowed brick stamped?Exact words, page and meaning recorded?

Here you record the whole source and judge it before it ever enters your essay. In Stops 34–35 your research log was the draft of this shelf; this shelf becomes the start of your literature review (Stop 39).

Read a catalogue card

CONTINUED
Project: How can dryland biodiversity in Uzbekistan be protected? — one entry from a student’s annotated bibliography (APA 7; the source is fictional, the card was written for this book).
The label
Karimova, D., & Holt, R. (2021). Dryland biodiversity under pressure: A review of threats in Central Asia. Caravan Journal of Ecology, 14(2), 101–118. https://doi.org/10.0000/cje.2021.0142
The card
(1) Karimova and Holt review recent research on threats to biodiversity in the deserts, steppes and riverside forests of Central Asia. (2) They identify habitat loss, invasive species and climate change as the three main pressures and argue that these act together rather than separately. (3) The article is a literature review rather than a field study: the authors compared about sixty published studies and organised them by type of threat and habitat. (4) Its main strength is its breadth, and its clear summary tables make a large field easy to map. (5) However, most of the studies it reviews were carried out outside Uzbekistan, and the authors admit that data on insects are scarce. (6) This source will be central to the literature review of my project, as it offers a framework of threats that I can use to organise my other sources. (7) I will need to supplement it with local studies, especially on pollinators.

Annotation: about 150 words · third person for the source, first person only in the “destination” sentences.

1. Write C, A, R or D for each sentence.

2. Which verbs does the writer use to report what the authors do?

3. (2) uses the present (identify, argue), but (3) the past (compared, organised). Why?

4. Find one strength and one limit. Are they specific or vague?

5. Why does the card not just say “This article is very useful”?

6. The card ends with …

a summary
a plan for the next search
a personal opinion

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: look only at the three titles and bylines. Which source will probably say most about workers’ health? Tick one.   A   B   C   · Three sources · about 645 words in all

Source A · The Office Is Not Dead. It Is Changing.

Dilnoza Rakhimova (2024) · a feature in Silk Road Business Monthly · fictional author and magazine, written for this book · about 205 words

A1When offices around the world emptied during the COVID-19 pandemic, many managers expected work to stop. It did not. Teams moved online, meetings moved to video calls, and a surprising amount of work carried on as before. Today the question is no longer whether people can work from home, but how much they should.

A2Many employers now admit that some tasks are done better at home. Without a daily commute or constant interruptions from colleagues, staff can concentrate on writing, analysing data or planning. Some firms have also noticed that they need less office space, which reduces their costs.

A3However, managers warn that remote work has a hidden price. New employees, in particular, learn much of their job by watching and asking experienced colleagues, and this is far harder through a screen. Creative ideas, too, often appear in unplanned conversations by the coffee machine rather than in scheduled online meetings.

A4For this reason, a growing number of organisations are choosing a hybrid model: staff spend some days in the office for teamwork and training, and the rest at home for focused tasks. The office, in other words, is not dead. It is becoming a place to meet rather than a place to sit.

Source B · Working Alone, Together

J. Turner & M. Yusupova (2024) · research review, Caravan Journal of Work and Society · fictional authors and journal, written for this book · about 220 words

B1Research on remote work and well-being presents a mixed picture. On the positive side, many studies suggest that the flexibility of working from home gives employees greater control over their day. Workers who no longer commute often report more time for family, exercise and sleep, and some describe lower levels of daily stress.

B2On the negative side, researchers have pointed out two related risks. The first is isolation: without casual contact with colleagues, some remote workers feel lonely and less connected to their organisation. The second is the loss of clear boundaries between work and private life. When the kitchen table is also the office, the working day may never quite end, and employees may answer messages late at night. Over time, this pattern can contribute to burnout.

B3Importantly, the effects of remote work are not the same for everyone. They appear to depend on conditions at home, such as having a quiet place to work, and on personal factors such as age, family responsibilities and personality. A young employee in a shared flat may experience remote work very differently from a parent in a large house.

B4Remote work, we argue, is therefore neither good nor bad in itself. Its effects depend on how it is organised, and we recommend clear routines and agreed limits on messages after working hours.

The third voice

CONTINUED

Source C · Clients Abroad, Desk at Home

Sardor Ismoilov (2024) · post on the blog Desk at Home · fictional, written for this book · about 220 words

C1Not long ago, a talented young designer in Samarkand or Nukus who dreamed of an international career often believed that the only way was to move abroad. Today, many young people in Uzbekistan work for foreign clients without leaving home. Programmers, designers, translators and online teachers find projects on international websites and are paid for work they do at their own desks.

C2For most of the freelancers I spoke to, the biggest advantage is opportunity. They can earn an international income while staying close to their families, and they can choose projects that match their skills. Several also point out that remote work allows them to continue their studies at the same time.

C3The challenges, however, are real. In some rural areas the internet connection is still slow or unstable, and a lost connection can mean a lost client. Because Uzbekistan is several hours ahead of Europe and North America, online meetings often take place late in the evening or at night. Freelancers also lack the security of a contract: when a project ends, the income ends too. Finally, many describe months of working alone as lonely.

C4Some have found a practical answer in coworking spaces, which are now opening in a number of cities, where freelancers can rent a desk, use a fast connection and meet people who do similar work.

Find one problem that Sources B and C share.
Jigsaw option. Groups A, B and C each become experts on one source: its main idea + three key points. Then, in mixed groups, find what the sources share and where they differ.

Language toolkit: summary language

10 MIN

A summary is full of other people’s voices. Reporting verbs tell your reader who is speaking and how strongly. Source linkers show how the voices relate to each other.

Notice find it

Find the reporting verbs in the sources and complete the sentences.

1. (A2) Many employers now that some tasks are done better at home.

2. (A3) However, managers that remote work has a hidden price.

3. (B1) … many studies that the flexibility of working from home …

4. (B2) … researchers have two related risks.

5. (B4) Remote work, we , is therefore neither good nor bad in itself.

What the verb tells your reader rule
MeaningReporting verbsIn a summary
neutralstates · notes · describes · reportsIsmoilov notes that many freelancers …
strongargues · claims · maintains · insistsTurner and Yusupova argue that …
cautioussuggests · indicatesResearch suggests that flexibility …
problemwarns · points out · admitsRakhimova warns that training new staff …

Source linkers: agreement — Both A and B note … · Like A, B … · Similarly, …  |  difference — A …, whereas B … · In contrast, … · Unlike A, B …  |  overall — Taken together, the sources suggest …

Four rules

  • Verb + that + clause, no about: Rakhimova notes that … ✓  ·  notes about that ✗
  • Tense (the Stop 23 rule): an author’s view → present (Rakhimova argues) · one study → past (Ismoilov interviewed freelancers) · the field → present perfect (researchers have pointed out)
  • According to X, + clause. According to Ismoilov, … ✓  ·  According to Ismoilov says … ✗
  • A plural subject takes a plural verb: Turner and Yusupova argue ✓  ·  argues ✗
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. According to Rakhimova says offices are changing.
2. Turner and Yusupova argues that routines help.
3. Ismoilov tells that freelancers often feel lonely.
4. Both Source B and C mentions isolation.

Level up: report with precision

CONTINUED

At C1 you keep each writer’s level of certainty, choose a verb that shows how they make a claim, and pack ideas into noun phrases. A summary says exactly what the sources say, no more and no less.

ToolPhrasesExample
Hedging
keeps a claim as careful as the source		appear to · tend to · may · it would seem thatRemote work appears to reduce daily stress for some employees.
Precise reporting
shows how a writer makes a claim		acknowledge · caution · contend · highlightRakhimova acknowledges that some tasks are done better at home.
Impersonal passive
reports a view without a name		It has been suggested that … · X is widely seen as …It has been suggested that hybrid schedules protect teamwork.
Nominalisation
verb or adjective → noun		isolate → isolation · flexible → flexibility · lose → lossWorkers no longer commute. → The loss of the daily commute gives workers more time.

The Blueprint: the honey bee

10 MIN

A summary from multiple sources is not three small summaries in a row. It is one new text, organised by ideas, not by sources — like honey from many flowers.

Leave out examples and details, group the key points by theme and add nothing that is not in the sources.

4 · Fill the honeycombGroup by themeThemes down, sources across: where do they agree? differ? Who adds what?
5 · One jar of honeyWrite the summaryTopic sentence → themes → overall sentence. A name in every point. No opinion.

A model summary

CONTINUED
Task: Summarise what Sources A–C say about how remote work affects workers’ well-being (about 130 words).
Step 4 · The honeycomb (model notes) notes
ThemeA · RakhimovaB · Turner & YusupovaC · Ismoilov
Benefitsno commuteflexibility → control; no commute → time for family, less stressstay near family; can keep studying
Risks—isolation; work–home boundaries blur → burnoutloneliness; night meetings (time zones); no contract
What helpshybrid: office days for contactroutines; limits on after-hours messagescoworking spaces
Step 5 · The jar (model summary, written for this book) model
Topic
Three recent sources consider how working from home affects the well-being of employees (Ismoilov, 2024; Rakhimova, 2024; Turner & Yusupova, 2024).
Theme 1
Both Rakhimova and Turner and Yusupova note that remote workers save time by not commuting, and Turner and Yusupova add that greater flexibility may reduce daily stress. Similarly, Ismoilov reports that young freelancers value staying close to their families.
Theme 2
However, the sources also identify clear risks. Turner and Yusupova warn that isolation and the loss of boundaries between work and home can lead to burnout, whereas Ismoilov highlights loneliness and late-night meetings with foreign clients.
Theme 3
All three writers propose practical solutions: hybrid schedules (Rakhimova), clear routines (Turner & Yusupova) and coworking spaces (Ismoilov).
Overall
Taken together, the sources suggest that remote work supports well-being only when it is carefully organised.
References

Two students summarised what Sources B and C say about the risks of remote work (about 60 words). Mark both.

Student A
Source B is about the risks of remote work. Turner and Yusupova (2024) note that some workers feel isolated and that the boundaries between work and home can disappear, which may lead to burnout. Both sources identify isolation as a key risk: Turner and Yusupova (2024) note that some remote workers feel cut off from their organisation, while Ismoilov (2024) reports that many freelancers find months of working alone lonely. Turner and Yusupova also caution that the loss of work–home boundaries may contribute to burnout, whereas Ismoilov highlights late-night meetings and the lack of a contract.

3

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: a research introduction ends with …   the answer   the questions   a joke

Scrolling, Not Reading? The Reading Habits of Second-Year Students

Section 1 · Introduction · a model research introduction by Malika Sobirova (fictional) · the student, the study and the sources it cites are fictional · about 460 words · written for this book

AReading has long been seen as one of the foundations of success at university. Students are expected to read widely: textbooks, articles, reports and, ideally, books they choose for themselves. Reading for pleasure, in particular, is often linked with a richer vocabulary, better writing and a stronger ability to concentrate. For students who study in a second or third language, regular reading may be even more important, because it offers contact with the language outside the classroom.

BIn recent years, however, the way young people read has changed considerably. Most students now carry a smartphone that offers news, messages, short videos and electronic books on the same small screen. Some commentators claim that this has created a generation that “scrolls rather than reads”, moving quickly from one short text to the next. Others argue that young people actually read more than ever before, but in different forms: posts, comments, online articles and e-books.

CResearchers in several countries have examined this question. Many studies have suggested that young adults spend less time reading printed books for pleasure than earlier generations did, and more time reading on screens (e.g., Harlow, 2019; Petrova & Kim, 2022). However, most of this research has been carried out in English-speaking countries and with school pupils rather than university students. Much less is known about university students in Central Asia, who often read in two or more languages and whose access to books, libraries and the internet may differ from that of students elsewhere.

DThis gap matters for teachers and for students themselves. If teachers want to encourage reading, they need to know what, how and why their students actually read today, rather than rely on general impressions. A common assumption such as “students do not read any more” may simply be wrong — or true only for some kinds of reading.

EThe present study therefore aims to investigate the reading habits of second-year students at one university in Uzbekistan. More specifically, it seeks to answer three research questions:

RQ1 How much time do second-year students spend reading for pleasure in a typical week?
RQ2 In which languages and formats (printed or digital) do they prefer to read?
RQ3 What reasons do students give for reading, or not reading, for pleasure?

While you read: underline every sentence that tells you what is not known yet. That is the gap — the reason this study exists. Remember: research is uncountable — we do research or conduct a study, never “a research”.
Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 4 · Practical class 38
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

FTo answer these questions, the study uses both primary and secondary sources. Primary data were collected through a short questionnaire completed by students from one faculty and through follow-up interviews with a small number of volunteers. Secondary sources — published studies and reports on reading habits — were used to place the findings in a wider context. Because the sample is small and comes from a single university, the results cannot be generalised to all students in Uzbekistan; rather, they are intended as a first step that larger studies could build on.

GThe paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews previous research on reading habits and digital reading. Section 3 describes the questionnaire and the interviews. Section 4 presents the results, and Section 5 discusses what they mean for students and teachers.

References (fictional sources, written for this book)
Harlow, R. (2019). Reading in the age of the screen: Young adults and their books. Minaret Press.
Petrova, A., & Kim, S. (2022). Print or pixels? Changes in young adults’ leisure reading. Journal of Reading on the Silk Road, 11(2), 45–61. https://doi.org/10.0000/jrsr.2022.045

Your research project: Stops 38–45

Topic menu

Pick one or bring your own. Keep it small: people you can reach, data you can collect in a week.

vocabulary apps · languages on social media · sleep before exams · part-time jobs · how we revise · buying clothes online · volunteering · the university library

Researching people: three rules

  • Ask permission. Say what it is for; people may say no.
  • Keep it anonymous. No names in your paper.
  • Ask only what you need. No sensitive personal questions (health problems, family income, religion, politics). Habits such as sleep or part-time work are fine if answers are anonymous and optional.
