Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: look at the bold headings. Is the review organised by …   author?   theme?

Switching Worlds: Multilingual Students at a Regional University

Section 2 · Literature review · N. Qodirova (2024), The Silk Road Review of Language and Education · the author, the journal and ALL studies cited are fictional · about 540 words · written for this book

AUzbekistan has long been a meeting point of languages. Uzbek is the state language, but Russian is still widely used, particularly in larger cities, in business and in some areas of higher education, and English has become an increasingly popular foreign language in recent years. Other languages, including Karakalpak, Tajik and Kazakh, are spoken by many people in particular regions and communities. For many young people, therefore, using more than one language is not an exception but part of ordinary life (Abdullayeva, 2018; Rasulova, 2023). This section reviews research on how university students use, and feel about, their languages. It is organised around three themes: language in everyday life, language in academic study, and attitudes and identity.

BLanguage in everyday life. Several studies have examined which languages young people use in different settings. Abdullayeva (2018), who interviewed students in two large cities, found that most participants used Uzbek at home and with older relatives but moved freely between Uzbek and Russian with friends. Similarly, Morgan (2020) observed that students at a university in the capital often mixed two languages within a single conversation, a practice known as code-switching. Both studies suggest that switching is a normal and skilful part of communication rather than a sign of weak language knowledge. Online communication appears to add a further layer: Ishida (2022) found that English words and phrases are common in students’ messages and social-media posts, even among students who rarely speak English aloud.

CLanguage in academic study. A second group of studies focuses on university learning. Tursunov and Haydarova (2021) found that many students read course materials in a language other than their medium of instruction, mainly because some specialist sources are more easily available in Russian or English. In contrast to the relaxed picture of everyday switching in Abdullayeva (2018), their participants described academic reading in a second language as tiring and slow. Morgan (2020) reached a similar conclusion, noting that students who followed lectures well sometimes struggled to write assignments in the same language. Taken together, these studies indicate that feeling comfortable in a language socially does not automatically mean feeling comfortable in it academically.

While you read: underline every reporting verb (found, observed, reports …) and circle every linker that joins two studies (similarly, both …). You will need them in the toolkit. How many linkers did you find in A–C?
Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 4 · Practical class 39
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

DAttitudes and identity. Research on attitudes paints a largely positive picture. Most participants in Ishida’s (2022) survey saw knowledge of several languages as an advantage for their careers, and many associated English in particular with international opportunities. Rasulova (2023), however, argues that language choice is also about who people feel they are. In her interviews, students explained that they used different languages to express different sides of themselves; as she puts it, “students do not simply switch languages; they switch roles” (p. 41). Whereas Ishida (2022) emphasises practical benefits, Rasulova (2023) draws attention to emotional and personal ones.

EThe gap. Although these studies offer a rich picture, they share three limitations. First, all of them were carried out in large cities, so less is known about students at smaller regional universities. Second, they relied on what students said about their language use rather than observing it directly. Finally, none of them examined how students’ language choices change during their years at university. The present study addresses the first of these gaps by investigating the language practices of students at a regional university.

References (fictional, written for this book)
Abdullayeva, D. (2018). Home, street and campus: Language choices of young city dwellers. Journal of Central Asian Language Studies, 6(1), 14–29.
Ishida, K. (2022). English online: Students’ messages and posts in a multilingual setting. Caravan Journal of Language Learning, 8(2), 51–66.
Morgan, L. (2020). Talking in two languages: Code-switching on a capital-city campus. Minaret Press.
Rasulova, S. (2023). Switching roles: Language and identity among Uzbek students. Oasis Studies in Linguistics, 9(1), 33–48.
Tursunov, B., & Haydarova, M. (2021). Reading for study in a second language. Minaret Studies in Education, 12(3), 101–117.

A C1 review does more than report. It shows how strong each finding is, judges the studies politely but firmly, and packs a whole idea into one noun phrase — so that the gap appears naturally.

Impersonal passive

Nominalisation
verb → noun		limit → limitation · rely on → reliance on · choose → choiceThey relied only on interviews. → Their reliance on interviews is a key limitation.

The Blueprint: the master builders’ bricks

A literature review is not a pile of summaries — one study, then the next, then the next. It is a wall: earlier studies laid in courses by theme, joined with mortar, with one brick missing — the gap your study will fill.

Group studies by theme, not one after another, and show how they relate.

Part of the wallPart of the reviewWhat you do
1 · The bricksEarlier studiesFor each source: author + year + its key finding (as in your Stop 37 summary)

3 · The mortarSynthesis languagesimilarly · both … and · in contrast · whereas · taken together
4 · The missing brickThe gapWhat have all these studies not done? (place, people, method, time)
5 · Your brickYour studyThe present study addresses this gap by …

Topic: learning English as a third language. Three studies (Karimov, 2019; Lewis, 2021; Nurmatova, 2022 — all fictional, written for this book). First, the builder fills a synthesis grid: studies down, themes across.

✗ The pile

Karimov (2019) interviewed 12 students. He found that they learn English for careers and travel and that Russian helped them with grammar. Lewis (2021) did a survey. She found that students learn English through games and films and make word-order errors. Nurmatova (2022) observed classes. She found that students learn English for exams and compare it with Russian.
Theme
Studies have suggested that students learn English as a third language for a mix of reasons.
Agree
Both Karimov (2019) and Lewis (2021) found that students link English with life outside the classroom: careers and travel in one study, games and films in the other.
Differ
In contrast, Nurmatova (2022) observed that many students study English mainly for exams and to meet their parents’ expectations.
Combine
Taken together, these studies suggest that practical and personal motives work side by side.

References (fictional, written for this book) · Karimov, J. (2019). Why English? Third-language learners at Uzbek universities. Silk Road Academic Books. · Lewis, H. (2021). Games, films and grammar: How students meet English. Caravan Journal of Language Learning, 7(2), 60–74. · Nurmatova, G. (2022). Exams, parents and English: A classroom study. Minaret Studies in Education, 13(1), 25–40.

1. How is the pile organised? How is the wall organised?

2. Circle the mortar in the wall: three linkers.

3. The wall leaves out “12 students” and “did a survey”. Why?

Copied line → Own words

8 MIN

In a literature review, most of what you report is paraphrased: new structure, new words, same idea — and always a citation. Quote only when the exact words matter, and add the page. All four sources below are fictional.

Valiyeva (2019, p. 12)“Young people in Central Asian cities often move between two or three languages in a single conversation without noticing it.”
→
According to Valiyeva (2019), for many young city dwellers in Central Asia, mixing languages while they talk is a frequent and largely unconscious habit.
Fischer (2021, p. 88)“Students rarely choose a language at random; each language carries its own social meaning.”
→
Hamidova (2020, p. 5)“Academic writing in a second language requires much more than good conversational skills.”
→
Osei (2018, p. 30)“The languages that parents choose at home have a strong influence on the languages their children later prefer.”
→

Tool tips: change the structure (verb ↔ noun, active ↔ passive) · use synonyms for ordinary words, keep key terms (code-switching) · start with the author: X (2021) points out that … · changing two words is not a paraphrase.

Phrase bank use these
JobB2 · safeC1 · upgrade
Open the reviewThis section is about …This section reviews research on … It is organised around three themes.
Report the fieldMany researchers studied …Several studies have examined … · Research has focused on …
Report one studyX (2020) found that …In a study of …, X (2020) observed that …
AgreeBoth X and Y … · Similarly, …This is consistent with … · X’s findings are corroborated by Y.
DifferIn contrast, … · Whereas X …, Y …Unlike X, Y … · These findings diverge from those of X.
QuoteX says: “…” (p. 41).As X puts it, “…” (p. 41).
Show the gapNobody has studied …However, none of these studies … · The present study addresses this gap by …

Be the examiner

Examiners use four criteria. Apply them first to two students’ paragraphs, then to your own literature review.

CriterionA C1 literature review …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear focus from the first brick to your brick
O · Organisationhas one idea per paragraph (theme → agree → differ → combine → gap) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students used the Level 2 notes to write a second course: How do people feel about switching? (about 60 words). Mark both.

Student A
Azimova (2019) found that students find it helpful when teachers switch to Uzbek. Clarke (2021) found that advanced students prefers English-only lessons. Yuldashev (2023) found that teachers feel guilty about switching because school rules say “English only”. These three studies are about feelings.
Student B
Attitudes towards switching appear to be mixed. Students in Azimova’s (2019) study found it helpful, whereas Clarke (2021) reported that advanced learners preferred English-only lessons. Teachers seem uneasy: Yuldashev (2023) draws attention to the guilt they feel when school rules demand “English only”. Taken together, these studies suggest that switching is valued in practice but not always accepted in principle.

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

2 · Word Bazaar

Wall sentence: the second one.
1 The pile goes study by study; the wall goes by theme (theme → agree → differ → combine). · 2 Both … and · In contrast · Taken together. · 3 Method details do not answer the theme question. · ☆ 4 e.g. Both Karimov (2019) and Nurmatova (2022) found that students compare English with Russian, whereas Lewis (2021) reported word-order errors caused by Uzbek. · 5 e.g. However, all three studies were carried out in large cities, so little is known about regional universities. · ☆ 6 open.

3

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: a methods section answers one big question. Which one? Tick it.   Why is this topic important?   How exactly was the study done?   What was found?

Little and Often: A Vocabulary App in the First-Year Classroom

Section 2 · Method · from a research article · about 620 words · C1 · The study, the authors and the journal are fictional, written for this book.

AThis study used a quasi-experimental design with three measurement points: a pre-test, a post-test and a delayed post-test. Its aim was to find out whether short daily practice with a vocabulary app helps first-year students to remember academic words better than the same amount of practice with printed word lists. Two existing classes were compared: one class used the app (the experimental group), while the other used paper lists (the control group). Because the students were not randomly assigned to the groups, differences between the two classes cannot be fully ruled out; this limitation is discussed in Section 5.

BThe participants were 58 first-year students of English at a university in Uzbekistan. They were recruited from two parallel groups taught by the same teacher, so that their regular lessons would be as similar as possible. All 64 students in the two groups were invited to take part during a normal class, and it was explained that participation was voluntary and would not affect their grades. Fifty-eight students agreed and signed a consent form. They were aged between 18 and 21, and all of them spoke Uzbek as their first language. According to the university’s placement test, their English was at B1 to B2 level.

CThe target words were selected from the reading texts of the students’ coursebook. First, 120 academic words were listed. This list was then tested with a pilot group of 15 second-year students, and words that more than half of them already knew were removed. The remaining 90 words were used in both groups. The experimental group practised the words in a free spaced-repetition app, which shows each word again after longer and longer intervals — for example, after one day, three days and a week. The control group received exactly the same words, definitions and example sentences on printed sheets. A 40-item test was designed: in 20 items, students wrote the meaning of a word; in the other 20, they completed a gapped sentence. Three versions of the test were prepared, each with the items in a different order.

Count the passives. Who did these things, and why does the writer not say?

Words to help you: quasi-experimental — like an experiment, but the groups were not formed at random · delayed post-test — a test given some weeks after the study ends · pilot group — a small group used to try out materials first · placement test — a test that decides a student’s level · retain — keep in memory

A methods section contains no results and no evaluation: only what was done, how and why.
Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 4 · Practical class 40
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

DThe study lasted eight weeks. In Week 1, the pre-test was administered to both groups in class, under the same conditions and with a 30-minute time limit. The app was then installed on the experimental group’s phones, and a short training session of about 15 minutes was given by the researcher. Both groups were asked to practise for ten minutes a day, five days a week. Practice time was recorded automatically by the app; the control group recorded theirs in a simple paper diary. In Week 8, the post-test was given under the same conditions. Four weeks later, a delayed post-test was administered without warning, to find out whether the words had been retained over a longer period. Finally, eight volunteers from each group were interviewed for about ten minutes. The interviews were conducted in Uzbek, recorded with the students’ permission and later translated into English.

EAll test papers were marked by two teachers who did not know which group each student belonged to. Where their scores differed, the paper was discussed until an agreement was reached. The mean scores of the two groups were then compared at each of the three test points. The interview recordings were transcribed and read several times, and recurring ideas, such as motivation, boredom and the role of reminders, were grouped into themes.

FBefore the study began, permission was obtained from the head of the department. All data were stored on a password-protected computer and made anonymous: each student was given a code, and no names appear in this article. When the study ended, the app was offered to the students in the control group, so that neither group was disadvantaged.

Jigsaw option. Group A: A–B (design, people) · Group B: C–D (tools, steps) · Group C: E–F (analysis, ethics). List every number in your part and what it describes; teach it to a new group.

How it works rule
FormExample from the textWhen to use it
was / were + past part.The pre-test was administered in Week 1.every finished step
… + by + the doermarked by two teachers who did not know …only when WHO matters

active past simpleThe study lasted eight weeks.when the subject really acts

Three rules

  • Agree: the test was given · the tests were given · the data were stored
  • Participles: given · chosen · held · taught · written · sent · sought
  • Never passive: participate, consist of, agree, happen → ✗ were participated

A C1 method explains why each choice was made, names its limits honestly and packs a step into a noun phrase — so that a reader trusts it and can repeat it.

ToolPhrasesExample
Past passive
the step, not the researcher		was administered · were recruited · was obtainedConsent was obtained from all participants.
Justifying a choice
says why a step was taken		in order to · so that · to ensure thatThe items were reordered to ensure that students could not copy.
Hedging limits
admits a weakness honestly		cannot be fully ruled out · may have influenced · it is possible thatThe small sample may have influenced the results.
Nominalisation
verb → noun		recruit → recruitment · collect → data collection · analyse → analysisWe collected the data in March. → Data collection took place in March.

Dilnoza is a second-year student (and a fictional one). Her mini-project asks: How do second-year students use vocabulary apps outside class? Here is the first draft of her methods section (written for this book). Read it, then check every rung.

(1)
This small study used an online questionnaire and one follow-up interview.
(2)
The participants were 34 second-year students of English from two groups at my faculty. All 46 students in the two groups were invited through the groups’ Telegram channels, and 34 completed the questionnaire (a response rate of 74%).
(3)
The questionnaire contained 12 questions: eight multiple-choice questions about how often, when and why students used vocabulary apps, and four open questions. Before it was sent out, it was piloted with three classmates, and two unclear questions were rewritten.
(4)
The link was posted on 3 March and was left open for one week. A reminder was sent after four days. After that, one student who used an app every day was interviewed for 15 minutes.
(5)
The multiple-choice answers were counted in a spreadsheet and turned into percentages. The open answers were read twice and grouped into topics. Most students said that they used apps on the bus, which shows that apps are perfect for busy people.
(6)
The questionnaire was anonymous, and no names or e-mail addresses were collected.

1. Write the rung number (1–6 from the ladder) in each box.

2. One sentence is a result, not a method. Underline it. Which section of the project does it belong in?

☆3. Why does Dilnoza give the response rate (74%)?

4. A rung is weak: what ethical step is missing for the interview?

5. Replication test: what else would you need to repeat her study? Where should she put it?

☆6. Find six past passives. Write them here.

☆7. Dilnoza’s draft is B2+. Upgrade two of its sentences with the Level-up tools (a reason for a choice, a hedged limit, nominalisation).

Tip: put your full questionnaire in an appendix. Your methods say what kind of questions you asked; the appendix shows every word — and it goes into your research portfolio (Stop 45).

Word Bazaar

8 MIN

Twelve words for reporting what was done in a study, step by step. Read the cards. Say each word aloud and make a sentence about a study on your campus.

phaseNOUN one stage of a study or a projectthe second phase of the study
baselineNOUN the situation measured before any change is madea two-week baseline
protocolNOUN a written plan of exactly how each step must be donefollow the protocol
briefingNOUN a short meeting that gives people instructionsa 30-minute briefing
sessionNOUN a period of time used for one activitya one-hour session
routineNOUN the same steps done in the same order each timethe evening routine
logVERB write numbers or events in an official recordlog the counts
assignVERB give someone a task, or put them in a groupassign tasks to assistants

excludeVERB leave out on purposeexclude the data for one day
sortVERB put things into groups by typesort bottles by colour
contaminateVERB make a material impure by adding something unwantedFood can contaminate a batch.

Level up · C1 words: standardise (make a step the same every time) · deviation (a change from the planned procedure) · sequential (happening in a fixed order) · contaminant (something that makes a material impure)

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: skim the first words of paragraphs B, C, D and E. What do they tell you about the order of the text? Write one sentence.

Better Labels, Cleaner Bins? A Campus Recycling Study

Section 2.3 · Procedure · from a research article · about 470 words · C1 · The study, the authors and the journal are fictional, written for this book.

AThe study was carried out over eight weeks in the spring semester and consisted of three phases: preparation (Weeks 1–2), a baseline phase with the original bin labels (Weeks 3–4) and an intervention phase with new picture labels (Weeks 5–8). Two buildings of the same faculty took part. In Building 1, the labels were changed at the start of Week 5, while in Building 2 the original labels were kept throughout, so that the two buildings could be compared over the same weeks.

BIn Week 1, written permission was obtained from the dean’s office and from the company that empties the bins. Three research assistants, all second-year students, were then trained in a 30-minute briefing. During the briefing, each assistant was given a printed protocol, which listed every step of the evening count in order, and the assistants practised the count together on two bins until their numbers matched.

CIn Week 2, the new labels were piloted. Ten students who were not involved in the study were shown two designs and asked which bin they would choose for six everyday items, such as a juice bottle with its cap still on. The design that led to fewer wrong choices was printed in A4 size and laminated. It was not put up, however, until the start of the intervention phase.

DFrom Week 3 onwards, the same routine was repeated every weekday evening. At 6 p.m., after the last classes had ended, the twelve plastic bins in the two buildings were checked by the assistants. Each item was taken out, sorted and logged on a paper form in one of three groups: plastic bottles in the right bin, plastic bottles in the wrong bin, and other items, which were counted as contaminants. Once the counts had been logged, the bins were emptied into the company’s collection bags, so that every count started from an empty bin.

Circle every time marker. Box every was / were + past participle. Which step was repeated?

Words to help you: the dean’s office — the office of the head of a faculty · laminated — covered with thin plastic for protection · intervention — the change a study tests (Stop 40) · torn — damaged by pulling

Jigsaw option. Group A: A–B (plan, preparation) · Group B: C–D (pilot, the evening routine) · Group C: E–G (the change, deviations, the end). Draw your steps on a time line (Weeks 1–8) and the routine as a wheel; explain them to a new mixed group without looking at the text.
☆Talk after reading: Why did the team make no announcement in Week 5? Would you have done the same?
Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 4 · Practical class 41
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

EOn the Monday of Week 5, the new labels were attached to all six plastic bins in Building 1 before 8 a.m., when the first classes began. No announcement was made, because the aim was to test the labels on their own, not a campaign. The evening routine then continued in both buildings for four more weeks.

FTwo deviations from the protocol occurred. On one day in Week 6, the bins in Building 2 were emptied by cleaners before the count; the data for that day were therefore excluded for both buildings. In Week 7, one label was torn, and it was replaced the next morning.

GAfter the last count, a five-item questionnaire was given to 60 students in Building 1 to find out whether they had noticed the new labels. Finally, the assistants were debriefed, and a short summary of the findings was sent to the dean’s office and to the cleaning company.

Remember from Stop 40: methods are reported in the past passive. A procedure adds exact time markers: when, in what order, how long, how often.

Notice find it

How it works rule
JobTime markersExample
When exactlyIn Week 1 · On 3 March · At 6 p.m.In Week 1, permission was obtained.
How long, how oftenfor four weeks · every eveningchecked every weekday evening
From · untilFrom Week 3 onwards · not … untilnot put up until Week 5
An earlier steponce / after + had (been) + p.p.Once the counts had been logged, …
The last stepFinally, · After the last count,Finally, the assistants were debriefed.

Three rules

  • Text order = time order (Stop 30): give the steps in the order they happened.
  • Earlier step → past perfect: Once the counts had been logged, the bins were emptied.
  • for + a period · during + a noun: ✗ during four weeks → ✓ for four weeks

Nodira (a fictional student) asked: Do students refill their own bottles at the faculty’s new water station? On the left are the notes she kept while collecting her data; on the right is the procedure she wrote from them (written for this book).

2 Mar: permission — dean’s office ✓
obs. sheet piloted 1 h (Fri) → 2 columns added
6–17 Mar · Mon–Fri · 12:00–13:00 (busiest)
every fill → own bottle / new bottle / cup
very cold hall, wore my coat!
end of each session: photo of sheet → totals in spreadsheet
15 Mar: station broken → no data
17 Mar: 5 interviews (most frequent users) · consent ✓
(1) The data were collected over two weeks in March, through observation at the faculty’s new water station and five short interviews. (2) On 2 March, permission for the observation was obtained from the dean’s office. (3) An observation sheet was then piloted for one hour, and two columns were added to it. (4) From 6 to 17 March, the station was observed every weekday from 12:00 to 13:00, the busiest hour of the day. (5) Each time a container was filled, its type was recorded: the student’s own bottle, a newly bought bottle or a paper cup. (6) At the end of each session, the sheet was photographed, and the totals were entered into a spreadsheet. (7) On 15 March, the station was out of order, so no data were collected that day. (8) Finally, on 17 March, five students who had used the station most often were interviewed, after their consent had been obtained.

1. Which sentence is the hub? What does it tell the reader?

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own procedure.

CriterionA C1 procedure …

V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: the past passive with time markers (were checked every evening, once … had been logged)

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: look at Figure 1. Which group changed most?   16–24   25–39   40–59   60+

Online at Every Age? Internet Use across Four Age Groups

Section 3 · Results · from a research article · about 530 words · C1 · The study, the journal and ALL the numbers are fictional (invented example data for practice, not real statistics) · written for this book.

AThis section presents the results of five annual surveys (2020–2024). Figure 1 shows the percentage of respondents in each age group who reported using the internet every day, and Table 1 gives the average number of hours that daily users spent online. Interview findings are reported at the end of the section.

BOverall, daily internet use increased in all four age groups over the five-year period, but the size of the increase varied considerably with age. As Figure 1 shows, the youngest group started from a very high level: 90% of respondents aged 16–24 were online every day in 2020, and this figure rose slowly to 97% in 2024. Among 25–39-year-olds, daily use climbed steadily from 80% to 92%.

CThe most striking changes were found among older respondents. In the 40–59 group, the proportion of daily users rose from just over half (52%) to almost three quarters (74%). The sharpest rise, however, was recorded among respondents aged 60 and over. In 2020, only 12% of this group used the internet every day. The figure increased slightly to 15% in 2021 and then rose sharply, reaching 41% in 2024 — more than three times the 2020 level. Even so, the majority of older respondents (59%) were still not daily users at the end of the period.

Every number in the text — can you find it in the figure or the table?

Figure 1. Respondents who used the internet every day, by age group, 2020–2024 (%) · INVENTED EXAMPLE DATA FOR PRACTICE — NOT REAL STATISTICS

Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 4 · Practical class 42
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

Table 1. Average hours online per day (daily users), by age group · INVENTED EXAMPLE DATA FOR PRACTICE — NOT REAL STATISTICS

Age group202020222024Main online activity (2024)
16–245.0 h6.1 h5.6 hmessaging and social media
25–393.6 h4.2 h4.1 hmessaging and work
40–591.9 h2.3 h2.6 hreading the news
60+0.6 h0.9 h1.2 hvideo calls with family

DTable 1 shows a different pattern for the amount of time spent online. The youngest group spent by far the most time on the internet, but their average did not rise continuously: it increased from 5.0 hours a day in 2020 to a peak of 6.1 hours in 2022 and then fell slightly to 5.6 hours in 2024. For 25–39-year-olds, the average rose from 3.6 to 4.2 hours and then remained almost stable (4.1 hours). In contrast, the two older groups showed a steady increase in both periods. Respondents aged 60 and over doubled their daily time online, from 0.6 to 1.2 hours, although this was still less than a quarter of the time spent by the youngest group.

EThe main online activity also differed by age. Messaging and social media were the most common activities for respondents under 25, while those aged 25–39 most often mentioned messaging and work. For the 40–59 group, reading the news was the top activity, and for the oldest group it was video calls with family members.

FIn the interviews, older participants most often said that they had started to use the internet in order to stay in touch with relatives who lived far away; none of them mentioned work as the main reason. Several young participants, in contrast, said that they had deliberately tried to spend less time on their phones.

GIn summary, three main findings emerged. First, daily internet use grew in every age group, but most strongly among respondents aged 60 and over. Second, the time spent online rose steadily in the two older groups, while it levelled off or fell slightly among younger respondents. Third, the main purpose of going online differed clearly by age, from social media among the youngest to video calls with family among the oldest. These findings are discussed in Section 4.

Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on Figure 1 and paragraphs B–C, Group B on Table 1 and D–E, Group C on A, F and G (the frame, the interviews and the summary). Each group checks every number in its part against the figure or the table. Then teach your part to a new mixed group in 60 seconds.

Language toolkit: describing data

10 MIN

Data language has two patterns. You can describe a change with a verb + adverb (rose sharply) or with an adjective + noun (a sharp rise). Good writers mix both. Results are usually reported in the past simple.

Notice find it

Complete these phrases from the text.

1. (B) … this figure to 97% in 2024.

2. (B) … daily use from 80% to 92%.

3. (C) The rise, however, was recorded among respondents aged 60 and over.

4. (D) … to a of 6.1 hours in 2022 and then to 5.6 hours.

5. (D) … the average rose from 3.6 to 4.2 hours and then (4.1 hours).

6. (D) Respondents aged 60 and over their daily time online …

How it works rule
Changeverb + adverbadjective + nounSize words
↑ uprose / increased / climbeda rise / an increasesharply · sharp
↓ downfell / decreased / declineda fall / a decrease / a declineconsiderably · considerable
→ no changeremained stable / levelled offa period of stabilitysteadily · steady
∧ toppeaked at / reached a peak ofa peakslightly · slight
PrepositionsExample
from … to … (start and end)Daily use rose from 12% to 41%.
by (the size of the change)It rose by 29 percentage points.
of (after a noun)a rise of 29 points · a peak of 6.1 hours

Three rules

  • rise ≠ raise: numbers rise / rose / have risen (no object). People raise prices.
  • Singular after “the number of”: the number of users has doubled · the majority of users were …
  • Adverb with a verb, adjective with a noun: ✗ a sharply rise · ✗ rose sharp
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. The number of daily users raised sharply.
2. Daily use increased on 12 percentage points.
3. The number of older users have doubled.
4. There was a sharply rise in 2022.

Level up: precise data language

CONTINUED

At C1 a results section does more than list numbers. It turns changes into noun phrases, compares groups in one sentence, uses proportion words that match the figures, and reports without explaining.

ToolPhrasesExample
Nominalised change
the change is the subject		there was a sharp rise in … · a threefold increase · reached a plateauA threefold increase in daily use was recorded among respondents aged 60+.
Comparison
two groups in one sentence		whereas · compared with · by far the most · twice as … asThe youngest group spent by far the most time online, whereas the oldest spent the least.
Approximation
words match numbers		just over half · almost three quarters · a small minorityAlmost three quarters (74%) of the 40–59 group were daily users.
Reporting
no explaining		was recorded · emerged · Even so, … · with the exception of …Three main findings emerged. Even so, most older respondents were not daily users.

Headlines shout and exaggerate. A results section is calm and exact: it gives the real number and claims no more than the data show. Use Figure 1 and Table 1.

news headlineGRANDPARENTS TAKE OVER THE INTERNET!

news headlineTeens glued to their phones 24/7
→
news headlineYoung people are finally logging off

Common traps

✗ The number of users raised.
✓ The number of users rose.
✗ Use increased on 10%.
✓ 40% → 50%: rose by 10 percentage points (the gap between two percentages) — or by 25% (the relative change). Not the same!
✗ In 2020 year, …
✓ In 2020, …
✗ 41 percents of respondents …
✓ 41 per cent (41%) of respondents …
✗ The majority of respondents uses phones.
✓ The majority of respondents use phones.
✗ Old people love video calls because …
✓ For the oldest group, the main activity was video calls.
✗ The number of users were increased.
✓ The number of users increased.
✗ It is seen from the table that …

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own results section.

CriterionA C1 results section …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear focus from the first window to the last: it reports, it does not explain
O · Organisationhas one idea per paragraph (Point → Big picture → Key numbers → Compare → Exceptions) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: describing data (rose sharply / a sharp rise, from … to, by, the number of … has)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students described Table 1 (average hours online per day). Mark both.

Student A
Table 1 shows the average hours online per day of daily users. Overall, the youngest group spent the most time online. In 2020 year they were online 5.0 hours, in 2022 the time raised to 6.1 hours and in 2024 it was fallen to 5.6 hours. The time of the 60+ group raised on 0.6 hours, from 0.6 to 1.2 hours, because they like video calls. The number of hours of all groups were increased.
Student B
Table 1 presents the average daily time online of respondents who used the internet every day. Overall, the youngest group spent by far the most time online throughout the period, whereas the oldest spent the least. Time online among 16–24-year-olds peaked at 6.1 hours in 2022 before falling slightly to 5.6 hours, while the figure for the 60+ group doubled, from 0.6 to 1.2 hours. Even so, the oldest respondents still spent less than a quarter of the time online that the youngest did.

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

3

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: a discussion section comes after the results. Which question does it answer? Tick one.   What happened?   What does it mean?   How were the data collected?

Why Do Students Keep Buying Clothes?

The writers never say “this proves”. Look for their careful words.
The discussion section of a student research paper + a reviewer’s response · about 610 words · C1 · The study, its authors and every study it cites are fictional · written for this book.

AThe aim of this study was to find out how often second-year students buy clothes and what drives their decisions. The most striking finding was that online discounts, rather than real need, were the main reason for most purchases: almost two-thirds of the 80 participants said that they had bought an item “because it was on sale”, and many of them admitted that they had worn it only once or twice.

BOne possible explanation for this pattern lies in the design of shopping apps. Several interviewees described receiving notifications late in the evening, often when they were tired after classes. It is likely that these timed messages encourage impulse buying, because they reach students at the moment when self-control tends to be lowest. However, as the study did not track actual app use, this interpretation should be treated with caution.

CThe results appear to be broadly consistent with earlier research. Like Saidova and Brandt (2020), who surveyed young shoppers in three Central Asian cities, we found that low prices mattered more than quality or brand. In contrast to their study, however, our participants rarely mentioned social media influencers. This difference may reflect the age of our sample: students who are busy with exams may follow fewer fashion accounts than the slightly older working shoppers in the earlier study.

DA less expected finding concerns second-hand clothing. Although many participants said that they cared about the environment, only a few had ever bought used clothes, and several connected them with embarrassment. This gap between attitude and behaviour has been reported in other studies of sustainable consumption (e.g., Okafor, 2019), and it suggests that information alone is unlikely to change shopping habits. Interestingly, students whose families regularly used a local tailor reported buying fewer new garments. It is possible that a tradition of repairing and altering clothes — still common in many Uzbek mahallas — offers a familiar alternative to disposable fashion.

ESeveral limitations should be acknowledged. First, the sample was small and came from one university, so the findings cannot be generalised to all young people in Uzbekistan. Second, the data were self-reported: participants may have remembered their purchases inaccurately or presented themselves in a positive light. Finally, the questionnaire did not ask what happened to clothes after they were worn, which limits what can be said about textile waste.

While you read: find one careful word or phrase (a hedge or a careful quantity) in each paragraph A–E.

A   B   C   D   E

Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 4 · Practical class 43
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

FDespite these limitations, the findings have some practical implications. Universities could include short workshops on consumer awareness in first-year programmes, and student unions might organise clothes swaps or repair days, building on the tailoring tradition mentioned above. Future research could follow a larger group of students over a full academic year and compare reported purchases with real shopping data. Such work would show whether the patterns observed here are temporary or part of a wider change in how young people consume clothing.

References (fictional sources, written for this book)
Okafor, T. (2019). Green words, old habits: The attitude–behaviour gap in sustainable consumption. Caravan Review of Social Science, 13(2), 41–58.
Saidova, M., & Brandt, K. (2020). Price, quality or brand? Young shoppers in three Central Asian cities. Journal of Consumer Studies on the Silk Road, 5(1), 12–29.

A reviewer responds

GThis is a clear and honest discussion. The writers restate their main finding, compare it with earlier work and admit the weaknesses of a small, self-reported sample. Two points, however, need attention. In paragraph B, the link between evening notifications and impulse buying is attractive, but it rests on a handful of interviews; even the word likely may be too strong, and saying that the notifications “might play a role” would match the evidence better. Secondly, the tailoring idea in paragraph D is the most original part of the paper, yet it receives only two sentences. Did these students buy less because of the tradition — or simply because their families had less money to spend? The writers should consider this alternative explanation before they recommend repair days. With these changes, the discussion would be both careful and convincing.

Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on A–B, Group B on C–D, Group C on E–F, Group D on G (the reviewer). Agree on the job of your part in five words, then teach it to a new mixed group in 60 seconds.

Language toolkit: hedging and comparing

10 MIN

Two jobs: turn the certainty down to match your evidence (hedging) and hold your results up to a mirror (earlier studies).

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the text and complete them.

1. (B) It is that these timed messages encourage impulse buying …

2. (C) The results to be broadly consistent with earlier research.

3. (C) their study, however, our participants rarely mentioned …

4. (C) This difference reflect the age of our sample …

5. (D) … it that information alone is unlikely to change shopping habits.

6. (D) It is that a tradition of repairing and altering clothes …

The certainty dial and the mirror rule
ToolWordsExample
Modal verbsmay · might · couldThis may reflect the age of the sample.
Careful verbssuggest · indicate · appear to · tend toThe results suggest that price matters.
Likelihoodit is likely / possible that · probablyIt is possible that tailoring helps.
Careful quantitysome · many · most · a fewMany participants … (not all of them)
Mirror: agreeis consistent with · is in line withThis is in line with Okafor (2019).
Mirror: differin contrast to · unlike · differs fromUnlike the earlier study, we found …

Three rules

  • One hedge is enough: may possibly perhaps suggest ✗ → may suggest ✓
  • Hedge claims, not facts: Eighty students took part. No hedge — you counted them.
  • Mirror prepositions: consistent with · in line with · in contrast to · unlike + noun
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. These results prove that all students love sales.
2. Our findings are consistent to earlier studies.
3. The data may possibly perhaps show a change.
4. Unlike to earlier studies, we found few influencers.
5. It is likely that 80 students took part in the survey.

Remember from Stop 23 · mirror tenses: one study → past simple (Saidova and Brandt (2020) found …) · an author’s view → present simple (Okafor (2019) argues …) · the field → present perfect (Other studies have reported …)

Level up: the careful mirror

CONTINUED

At C1 a discussion does not only say may and consistent with. It measures how far results agree, chooses precise verbs for the mirror, considers other explanations and resists the tempting conclusion. Readers trust a writer who is bold about the data and honest about their limits.

ToolPhrasesExample
Degree words
how far results agree		broadly · largely · to some extent · in partOur results are broadly consistent with Okafor (2019).
Mirror verbs
agree or differ precisely		lend support to · corroborate · echo · diverge from · run counter toThese findings lend support to Saidova and Brandt (2020).
Alternative explanation
another possible cause		An alternative explanation is that … · It cannot be ruled out that …An alternative explanation is that these families simply had less money to spend.
Resisting the tempting claim
concession + limit		While it is tempting to conclude that …, … · Although …, the data do not show …While it is tempting to conclude that apps cause impulse buying, the evidence comes from a few interviews.

The Blueprint: light the lantern

10 MIN

At the top of a great minaret sits a lantern: a small room with arched windows, where, legend says, a light helped travellers find the tower at night. The discussion section is your lantern. It answers one question: so what?

Every study has a shadow: state its limitations yourself.

The lanternThe moveAsk yourself
1 · The flamerestate the key findingWhat did I find that matters most?
2 · The windowsinterpret itWhy might this be? What else could explain it?
3 · The mirrorcompare with earlier studiesDo other researchers agree? Where do we differ?
4 · The shadowadmit the limitationsWhere does my light not reach?
5 · The beamimplications + future researchWho can use this? What should be studied next?

Walk through the lantern

CONTINUED
Nodira’s mini-project (fictional, written for this book): Would students swap clothes instead of buying new ones? She organised a clothes-swap day at her faculty and asked 30 visitors to fill in a short questionnaire. Her results: 22 visitors said they would come again, but only 9 brought clothes to give away. Here is her discussion.
1 · The flame
(1) The main finding of this small study is that visitors were far more willing to take clothes than to give them: most said they would return, but fewer than a third brought items to swap.
2 · The windows
(2) One possible explanation is that many students do not own clothes they are ready to give away, especially if they live in a dormitory with a small wardrobe. (3) It is also possible that some visitors did not know they could bring items.
3 · The mirror
(4) This pattern is in line with Rahimov (2021), who observed a similar imbalance at swap events in Samarkand. (5) Unlike his study, however, mine found that visitors valued the social side of the event as much as the free clothes.
4 · The shadow
(6) These results should be interpreted with care. (7) Only 30 people took part, and all of them had already chosen to attend a swap event.
5 · The beam
(8) Nevertheless, the findings suggest that future swap days should be advertised earlier, so that students have time to collect clothes. (9) A larger study could compare swap events in several faculties.

Reference (a fictional source, written for this book) · Rahimov, S. (2021). Give one, take one: Clothes-swap events in Samarkand. Oasis Journal of Community Studies, 3(2), 77–90.

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own discussion.

CriterionA C1 discussion …
T · Taskanswers the exact question, keeps one clear position from the flame to the beam and claims no more than the data can show
O · Organisationhas one idea per paragraph (flame → windows → mirror → shadow → beam) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: hedging and comparing with earlier studies (may, suggest, consistent with, in contrast to)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Result (fictional): Eighteen of the 25 students had bought clothes in an online sale in the last month. Mark both.

Student A
The most important finding is that 18 of the 25 students bought clothes in an online sale. This proves that all students are addicted to sales, and shops must stop them. One possible explanation is that notifications arrive in the evening, when students are tired. This is consistent to Saidova and Brandt (2020), who found that price mattered more than quality. The sample was small, so future studies could ask more students.
Student B
The most striking finding was that almost three quarters of the participants (18 of 25) had bought clothes in an online sale during the previous month. One possible explanation is that sale notifications reach students when self-control tends to be low, although limited budgets may also play a role. This finding lends support to Saidova and Brandt (2020), who found that price mattered more than quality. Admittedly, the sample was small and self-reported; nevertheless, the results suggest that short consumer-awareness workshops may be worth trying.

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: this article has no abstract — you will collect the facts it would need. Skim the four headings. Where will you find the number of participants? Tick one.   Introduction   Method   Results   Discussion

Giving Time, Gaining Well‑being?

Volunteering and Life Satisfaction among University Students · D. Rahimova and J. Holt · Journal of Student Life Studies · a research article, shortened · about 530 words · C1 · The article, its authors, the journal and the numbers are fictional (invented data), written for this book.
No abstract here. Hunt for the facts each stripe needs — then do the same with your own project.

1 · Introduction

AVolunteering is often described as good for communities, but researchers have also asked whether it is good for the volunteers themselves. Many studies in different countries suggest that people who give their time to others tend to report higher life satisfaction. Most of this research, however, has focused on adults in Europe and North America. Far less is known about university students in Central Asia, who often combine study, family duties and part-time work.

BIn Uzbekistan, helping others has deep roots. The tradition of haşar, in which neighbours work together to build a house or clean a mahalla street, is still practised in many communities, and universities increasingly encourage students to take part in organised volunteering. The objective of the present study was therefore to examine whether regular volunteering is linked to the well-being of university students, and whether the type of activity matters.

2 · Method

CThe study took place at two universities in Uzbekistan during one academic semester. A total of 160 second- and third-year students took part: 80 who had volunteered at least twice a month during the previous year (the volunteer group) and 80 who had not volunteered (the comparison group). The two groups were similar in age, gender and field of study.

DAll participants completed an online questionnaire which measured life satisfaction, stress and sense of belonging on five-point scales. Volunteers also described the type of work they did. In addition, twelve volunteers were interviewed for about thirty minutes each, so that the numbers could be explained in the students’ own words.

3 · Results

EThe volunteer group reported significantly higher life satisfaction (t-test, p < .01) and a stronger sense of belonging (p < .05) than the comparison group. Levels of stress, however, were almost the same in both groups. Among the volunteers, those who worked directly with people — for example, tutoring children or visiting older residents — reported higher well-being than those who did practical tasks alone, such as sorting donations.

FThe interviews added an important detail. Many volunteers said that the greatest benefit was not the feeling of “doing good” but meeting people outside their usual circle. Several also mentioned that volunteering helped them to feel useful at a time when their studies seemed abstract and far from real life. A minority, however, described feeling tired and guilty when they could not balance volunteering with exams.

Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 4 · Practical class 44
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

4 · Discussion

GThese findings suggest that volunteering is associated with higher well-being among students, mainly through social contact and a sense of belonging. They are consistent with earlier international research, but they also add a local dimension: students who joined community activities that resembled haşar described them as a natural continuation of family values. The absence of a difference in stress suggests that volunteering is not a cure for academic pressure.

HThe study has clear limitations. Because it compared two existing groups, it cannot show that volunteering causes well-being; happier students may simply be more likely to volunteer. The data were also self-reported and came from only two universities. Future studies should follow students over time, ideally before and after they start volunteering. Meanwhile, universities may wish to support programmes that bring students into direct contact with people, while keeping such activities flexible during exam periods.

Jigsaw option. Four expert groups: Introduction (A–B), Method (C–D), Results (E–F), Discussion (G–H). Each group reduces its section to one sentence of no more than 30 words. Then form mixed groups of four and put your sentences together: this is a first draft of an abstract.

CONTINUED
A model abstract. K. Yusupova, “Haşar 2.0: Online Volunteering and Students’ Sense of Purpose”, Central Asian Review of Youth Studies. The article, author and journal are fictional, written for this book.
1 · Background
(1) Online volunteering, such as translating documents for charities or tutoring children by video, has grown in recent years, especially among young people, and traditional volunteering has often been linked to well-being, yet little is known about the benefits of online volunteering for the volunteers themselves.
2 · Aim
(2) This study examined whether online volunteering is associated with university students’ sense of purpose and loneliness, and what volunteers themselves value in it.
3 · Method
(3) A questionnaire measuring sense of purpose and loneliness was completed by 120 second- and third-year students at three universities in Uzbekistan, half of whom had volunteered online for at least three months; the other half had never volunteered. (4) Ten volunteers were also interviewed about their experience, and the interviews were analysed for recurring themes.
4 · Results
(5) Online volunteers reported a stronger sense of purpose than non-volunteers, but no difference was found in loneliness. (6) Volunteers who tutored children reported the strongest sense of purpose, while those who translated documents reported the weakest. (7) Interviewees valued the flexibility of online work and the chance to use their language skills, although several missed face-to-face contact with the people they helped.
5 · Conclusion
(8) The findings suggest that online volunteering may offer students a meaningful and flexible way to contribute, but it does not appear to replace the social benefits of traditional volunteering. (9) Universities could therefore combine online and face-to-face options and help new volunteers choose tasks that involve direct contact with others.
Keywords: online volunteering; sense of purpose; university students; Uzbekistan

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own abstract.

CriterionA C1 abstract …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear focus from the first stripe to the last, within the word limit

V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: tenses and concise noun phrases in abstracts (This study examined whether …; data were collected …; no difference was found in …)

Student A
Mentoring programmes are popular in universities, but there is not much information about first-year students in Central Asia. This study examine if mentoring helps students to feel that they belong and have less stress. 90 first-year students was answered a questionnaire, and half of them was in a mentoring scheme for one semester. Mentees felt more belonging, but the stress was not different. So mentoring can help all new students at university.
Student B
Peer mentoring is increasingly common at universities, yet little is known about its effects on first-year students in Central Asia. This study examined whether mentoring is associated with students’ sense of belonging and stress. Questionnaire data were collected from 90 first-year students, half of whom took part in a one-semester mentoring scheme. Mentees reported a stronger sense of belonging than other students, although no difference in stress was found. The findings suggest that mentoring may ease the transition to university life.

3

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: the essay asks “Which language is really ours?” What do you think the writer’s answer is? Tick one.   the mother tongue   English   there is no single answer

The Languages We Live In

An academic essay · about 600 words · C1 · written for this book
Paragraph F explains why editing matters. Find the sentence.

AAsk a student in Tashkent which language she speaks, and the answer may take a while. She might speak Uzbek with her grandparents, Russian with some university friends, English in her lectures and a mixture of all three in messages to her sister. For millions of people in Central Asia, and for a large part of the world’s population, using more than one language is not an exception but an ordinary part of daily life. This raises a question that linguists, psychologists and writers have discussed for centuries: if we live in several languages, which one is really “ours”?

BFor many people, the mother tongue holds a special place. It is the language of lullabies, family jokes and proverbs, and it carries a heritage that is passed from one generation to the next. When a language disappears, researchers often point out, a community loses more than a set of words; it may also lose songs, stories and ways of seeing the world. This is one reason why many countries try to preserve minority languages, from Welsh in Britain to Karakalpak in Uzbekistan.

CThe idea that language and identity are connected is not new in this region. In 1499, Alisher Navoi completed Muhokamat ul-lughatayn (“The Judgement of Two Languages”), in which he compared Turkic and Persian and argued that Turkic could express the finest poetry. At a time when Persian dominated literature, his argument was also a statement about who his readers were and what their own language deserved. More than five centuries later, his name is given to a city, countless streets and the national library — a reminder of how strongly one writer can shape the way a community sees its language.

DYet a second language does not necessarily threaten the first. Many bilingual speakers describe their languages not as rivals but as different rooms in the same house. Some say they feel more polite in one language, more direct in another and funnier in a third. Linguists call the habit of moving between languages within a conversation code-switching. Although it is sometimes criticised as “mixing” or laziness, research suggests that it is often a skilled choice: speakers switch to show closeness, to quote someone, or simply because one language has the more precise word.

EWriting in a foreign language adds another layer. When students write academic English, they are not only translating their thoughts; they are also learning a new register, with its own rules about articles, hedging and formality. Some feel that this voice is not really theirs. Others discover that it allows them to express ideas they had never put into words before. Both experiences are common, and both are part of becoming a writer in more than one language.

Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 4 · Practical class 45
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

FAccuracy matters here for a reason that goes beyond grades. Small errors — a missing article, a verb that does not agree with its subject, a comma in the wrong place — rarely destroy meaning, but they can distract a reader from it. An editor who checks these details is not erasing the writer’s identity. On the contrary, careful editing allows the writer’s own ideas, rather than the mistakes, to be heard.

GPerhaps, then, the question “Which language is really ours?” has no single answer. A person can belong to a mother tongue, grow inside a second language and build a professional voice in a third. The task of a multilingual writer is not to choose one language and abandon the others, but to use each of them with care — and to edit, patiently, until the words say exactly what is meant.

Jigsaw option. Group A: paragraphs A–B · Group B: C–D · Group C: E–G. Become experts on your part, then teach it to a new mixed group in 60 seconds. Group C must explain paragraph F in their own words.

Language toolkit: the four inspectors

10 MIN

Most red marks in a final draft come from four places: articles, agreement, punctuation, register.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the essay and complete them.

The four inspectors rule
InspectorChecks✗ → ✓
Artarticles: a / an = one of many · the = we know which · no article = in generalThe research shows → Research shows …
Agragreement: find the head noun · one of / each + singular verbOne of the students speak → One of the students speaks
Ppunctuation: comma after an opening linker · apostrophesHowever the results → However, the results · the students’ answers
Regregister: no contractions, slang or general “you”kinda, a lot of, get → rather, many, obtain

Three rules

  • One inspector at a time: read your text four times, once for each job.
  • Uncountable in English: research, information, evidence, feedback, advice — no -s, no a.
  • Read it aloud: your ear catches what your eyes miss.

Level up: editing for precision

CONTINUED

The four inspectors catch errors. A C1 editor goes further: she cuts words that add nothing, chooses the precise collocation, makes lists parallel and keeps the register steady from the first line to the last.

ToolEditExample
Cut redundancy
same meaning, fewer words		the reason is because → because · in order to → to · very unique → uniqueBilinguals switch because one language has the more precise word.
Precise collocation
the word that belongs		make a research → conduct research · big part → large proportionI conducted research on heritage languages.
Parallel structure
lists in the same form		to show …, to quote …, to fill … · not X but YSpeakers switch to show closeness, to quote someone or to fill a gap.
Steady register
no slips into chat		a lot of → many · think → believe · kinda → rather · you → peopleMany participants believe that English is rather formal.

Malika’s mini-project (fictional): How do students in Navoi switch between languages in their text messages? Here is one paragraph of her discussion with her teacher’s codes — and her final version.
Draft
with codes
The results showsAgr that the mostArt of participants switch between Uzbek and Russian in their messages. HoweverP they rarely use English, maybe because it is kindaReg formal for them. One of the intervieweeAgr said that English is “for exams, not for family”. This findingsAgr is consistent toWW Karimova (2022)*P who found a similar pattern among school students.
Teacher’s comment
Clear finding and a lively quotation — well done. Please check the eight codes. One question: do you need the quotation? It makes the paragraph longer.
Final version
The results show that most participants switch between Uzbek and Russian in their messages. However, they rarely use English, possibly because they associate it with formal situations. One of the interviewees said that English is “for exams, not for family”. This finding is consistent with Karimova (2022)*, who found a similar pattern among school students.

* Karimova (2022) is a fictional source, written for this book. Malika’s reference list: Karimova, N. (2022). Code-switching in school students’ text messages. Caravan Journal of Language Studies, 4(2), 33–47.

Common traps

✗ informations, researches, advices
✓ information, research, advice
✗ The students was very active.
✓ The students were very active.
✗ However the results were clear.
✓ However, the results were clear.
✗ I made a research about languages.
✓ I conducted research on languages.
✗ According to my opinion, …
✓ In my view, …
✗ We discussed about the results.
✓ We discussed the results.

Inspect a brick

In my study, I asked 40 student1 Agr about there2 Sp languages. The most3 Art of them speaks4 Agr Uzbek at home and Russian with friends. However5 P many participants said that English is a6 Art language of their future. I think it is super7 Reg interesting, because nobody have8 Agr asked them before.
LEVEL 2

Polish a wall

No codes this time. Find six errors (2 × Art, 2 × Agr, 1 × P, 1 × Reg). Write the code above each error, then copy the paragraph correctly.

Code-switching is common among young people in Uzbekistan. Many of my participants uses three languages every day, and each of them have a favourite language for jokes. Interestingly they said that the English is useful for career but not for family. Some of them also told me that switching languages felt a bit weird at first but quickly became normal.
Level 2 has no codes. Read the paragraph four times, once for each inspector.

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own final draft.

CriterionA C1 final draft …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear position from the foundation to the flag, acting on every piece of feedback
O · Organisationhas one idea per paragraph (finding → explanation → comparison) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: articles, agreement and punctuation (most participants · this finding is · However, …)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

The draft (with codes): The mostArt of participants speaksAgr Uzbek at home. HoweverP they usesAgr Russian with friends, maybe because it is kindaReg easier. This findingsAgr is consistent toWW Aliyeva (2021)*. Two students wrote the final version. Mark both.

Student A
The most of participants speak Uzbek at home. However they use Russian with friends, maybe because it is easier for them. This findings are consistent with Aliyeva (2021).
Student B
Most participants speak Uzbek at home. However, they tend to use Russian with friends, possibly because they associate it with informal settings. This finding is consistent with Aliyeva (2021)*, who reported a similar pattern among school students, although the present sample was considerably smaller.

* Aliyeva (2021) is a fictional source, written for this book: Aliyeva, D. (2021). Home and school languages of Uzbek teenagers. Silk Road Journal of Education, 9(1), 51–66.

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

Put your portfolio together in this order.

Pack your portfolio

1Title page — title, your name, group, date

MT12, out of 100: abstract parts 20 · accuracy 20 · language, length 10 · APA 7 10 · portfolio 25 · reflection 15.

Real data only in your portfolio. In class you may practise with invented numbers, marked “invented data”. The results in your MT11 text and in your research portfolio must come from data you really collected.
My reflective note 120–150 words

Look back at your minaret. Use the four starters — in your own order — and the phrase bank on the Chat → Final draft page.

Answer key · Stop 45

2 · Word Bazaar

Dominoes: preserve cultural heritage · switch between languages mid-sentence · a strong sense of belonging · your mother tongue · proofread for spelling mistakes · a formal register.
Odd one out: 1 publish (not an editing stage) · 2 foreign (the others mean the first language) · 3 chatty (informal; the others are academic).

3 · Case files

Before you read: there is no single answer.
Case 1: A iv · B viii · C i · D vi · E iii · F v · G ix (ii and vii are extra).
☆ Case 1b: 1 the fact that many people live in several languages · 2 Alisher Navoi’s · 3 code-switching · 4 the voice of academic English · 5 the languages a person uses.
☆ Case 1c: 1 preserve · 2 dominated · 3 heritage · 4 abandon · 5 register.
☆ Case 1d: 1 Yes · 2 No · 3 Not Given · 4 No.
☆ Case 2: 1 False · 2 True · 3 Not Given · 4 False · 5 True · 6 False · 7 True · 8 Not Given.
Case 3: 1 B · 2 C · 3 C · 4 A.
Case 4: 1 B · 2 B · 3 rivals.

4 · The four inspectors

Notice: 1 is · 2 the · 3 a · 4 a comma (laziness, research) · 5 is · 6 register.
Fix it: 1 Research shows that bilingual children learn fast. · 2 However, the students were unsure of their roots. · 3 Code-switching can be useful for students. · 4 Each of the interviewees speaks three languages. · 5 Most students prefer English in science.

4 · Level up

☆ Notice (any four): not an exception but an ordinary part (A) · lullabies, family jokes and proverbs (B) · not as rivals but as different rooms (D) · more polite …, more direct … and funnier … (D) · belong to …, grow inside … and build … (G) · not to choose … but to use … (G).
☆ Make it C1 (model answers): 1 They switch because it is quicker. · 2 I conducted research on heritage languages. · 3 Switching serves to show closeness, to quote people and to fill a gap when a word is missing. · 4 Many participants believe that English is rather useful. · 5 Uzbek is not only a home language but also a language of science.

5 · Blueprint and Malika’s ceremony

Accuracy comment: the second one.
Edit log: P × 2 — However, they … · Karimova (2022), who … · Reg + WW — kinda formal → associate it with formal situations; consistent to → consistent with · quotation — kept, as it shows the participants’ own voice.
1 The suggestion to delete the quotation; feedback is advice, and she explains her choice. · 2 thinking about every comment, then deciding. · ☆ 3 e.g. This finding lends support to Karimova (2022).

6 · Chat → Final draft (model answers)

2 Code-switching appears to be a normal part of everyday communication among the participants. · 3 The results suggest that some young people may attach less importance to their mother tongue. · 4 I found the feedback on articles particularly helpful.
☆ Error auction: 1 ✗ (… is limited) · 2 ✓ · 3 ✓ · 4 ✗ (Each of the families has its own rules).

7 · Writing ladder

Level 1: 1 students · 2 their · 3 Most · 4 speak · 5 However, · 6 the (language of their future) · 7 particularly · 8 has.
Level 2: uses → use (Agr) · each of them have → has (Agr) · Interestingly they → Interestingly, they (P) · the English → English (Art) · for career → for a career (Art) · a bit weird → somewhat unusual (Reg).

8 · Be the examiner (suggested)

Student A: T 2 (Art and P codes ignored; This findings not fixed) · O 2 · V 2 (maybe, easier for them) · G 1 (The most of, However they, This findings are). Student B: 3 · 3 · 3 · 3. Biggest difference: G.
☆ Be the editor: Most participants … · This finding is …
☆ Name the code: a Agr (were) · b Art (an important language) · c P (In addition, the …) · d Reg (Many children) · e WW (conducted / carried out an interview) · f Sp (their).

☆ Extra practice · Make it formal (model answers)
